# Kingston Line

The **Kingston Line** is a commuter rail line operated by the Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority (MBTA) in eastern Massachusetts. It runs from South Station in Boston to Kingston, serving the South Shore region. The line is part of the MBTA Commuter Rail system and is operated by Keolis Commuter Services .

Originally known as the **Plymouth/Kingston Line**, the service was restored in 1997 as part of the Old Colony Lines project, which reactivated passenger rail in the region for the first time since 1959 . The line formerly served a second terminus at Plymouth station; however, that station was indefinitely closed in April 2021 due to operational constraints and low ridership, leading to the line's renaming .

## History

### Old Colony Railroad and Closure
The route of the Kingston Line follows the alignment of the original Old Colony Railroad, which opened between Boston and Plymouth in 1845 . This corridor became a primary rail artery for southeastern Massachusetts. Passenger service on the Old Colony Division continued through the mid-20th century but began to decline with the rise of automobile travel. The New York, New Haven and Hartford Railroad, which had acquired the line, ceased all passenger service on the Old Colony Division in 1959 .

### Restoration (1997)
In the 1980s and 1990s, the Commonwealth of Massachusetts undertook the Old Colony Railroad Rehabilitation Project to restore commuter rail service to the South Shore. Construction began in 1993 . Service was officially restored on September 29, 1997, operating as the Plymouth/Kingston Line . This restoration occurred simultaneously with the reopening of the Middleborough/Lakeville Line. The project involved upgrading tracks, signals, and constructing new stations to modern accessibility standards .

### Plymouth Station Closure and Renaming
For the first 24 years of restored service, the line utilized a fork at its southern end. Trains would split after Halifax, with some proceeding to Kingston and others to Plymouth station at Cordage Park. This configuration presented operational challenges, as trains serving Plymouth often had to perform reverse moves or sequential stops (Kingston then Plymouth), which increased travel times .

In April 2021, amid service adjustments related to the COVID-19 pandemic and a review of low-ridership stations, the MBTA indefinitely closed Plymouth station . At the time of closure, ridership at Plymouth was significantly lower than at Kingston, which offers direct access to Massachusetts Route 3 and a large parking garage . Following the closure, the line was officially renamed the Kingston Line .

## Route and Stations

The Kingston Line runs 35.1 miles (56.5 km) from South Station to Kingston . The northern section of the line shares trackage with the Middleborough/Lakeville Line (renamed the Fall River/New Bedford Line in 2025) and the Greenbush Line as far south as Braintree .

From South Station, trains run south along the Southeast Expressway (Interstate 93), stopping at JFK/UMass and Quincy Center. After Braintree, the Kingston Line splits from the main line used by the Fall River/New Bedford Line and heads southeast through Weymouth, Abington, Whitman, Hanson, and Halifax . The line terminates at Kingston station, located near Route 3 .

### Station List

| Station | Zone | Municipality | Notes |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **South Station** | 1A | Boston | Terminus; connections to Amtrak, Red Line, Silver Line . |
| **JFK/UMass** | 1A | Boston | Connections to Red Line, bus services . |
| **Quincy Center** | 1 | Quincy | Connections to Red Line, bus terminal . |
| **Braintree** | 2 | Braintree | Connections to Red Line; split from Fall River/New Bedford Line . |
| **South Weymouth** | 3 | Weymouth | . |
| **Abington** | 4 | Abington | . |
| **Whitman** | 5 | Whitman | . |
| **Hanson** | 6 | Hanson | . |
| **Halifax** | 7 | Halifax | . |
| **Kingston** | 8 | Kingston | Terminus; located near Route 3 . |

*Former Station:* **Plymouth** (Zone 8) – Located at Cordage Park; closed indefinitely on April 5, 2021 .

## Operations

### Passenger Service
As of late 2025, the Kingston Line operates seven days a week. Weekday schedules typically feature peak-direction service during rush hours and bi-directional service during the midday and evening. Trains operate in a push-pull configuration using diesel locomotives . The trip from South Station to Kingston takes approximately one hour .

### Ridership
In October 2022, the line reported 4,171 average weekday boardings . By late 2025, the MBTA Commuter Rail system as a whole had recovered a significant portion of its pre-pandemic ridership, with over 100,000 daily weekday boardings system-wide .

### Freight Service
Freight operations on the line are managed by the **Massachusetts Coastal Railroad** (Mass Coastal). Historically, freight rights were held by the Bay Colony Railroad. In late 2023, Mass Coastal acquired the assets and freight rights of the Bay Colony Railroad, including the Kingston Line . Freight trains interchange with CSX Transportation at Braintree and serve customers along the line .

## Infrastructure

### Kingston Wind Turbine
In 2012, a wind turbine was installed at the Kingston layover facility, located adjacent to the Kingston station. The project, funded by a $2.5 million federal grant, was designed to generate electricity for the station lights and the layover facility, where trains are stored overnight . The turbine was projected to cover approximately 65% of the station's energy needs .

The **MBTA Commuter Rail** ([reporting mark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reporting_mark "Reporting mark") **MBTX**) system serves as the [commuter rail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commuter_rail "Commuter rail") arm of the [Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Bay_Transportation_Authority "Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority")'s (MBTA's) transportation coverage of [Greater Boston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greater_Boston "Greater Boston") in the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States"). Trains run over 429 mi (690 km) of track on 12 lines to 143 stations. It is operated under contract by [Keolis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keolis "Keolis").

In 2024, the system had a ridership of 30,343,900, or about 100,200 per weekday as of the third quarter of 2025, making it the [fifth-busiest commuter rail system in the U.S.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_United_States_commuter_rail_systems_by_ridership "List of United States commuter rail systems by ridership"), behind the three New York-area systems and the [Chicago-area system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metra "Metra"). The lines' characteristic purple-trimmed coaches operate as far south as [North Kingstown, Rhode Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Kingstown,_Rhode_Island "North Kingstown, Rhode Island"), and as far north as [Newburyport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newburyport,_Massachusetts "Newburyport, Massachusetts") and as far west as [Fitchburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fitchburg,_Massachusetts "Fitchburg, Massachusetts"), both in [Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts "Massachusetts").

Trains originate at two major [terminals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terminal_station "Terminal station") in [Boston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston "Boston") – [South Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Station "South Station") and [North Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Station "North Station"). The only connection between the two halves of the system is the non-revenue [Grand Junction Branch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Junction_Railroad_and_Depot_Company "Grand Junction Railroad and Depot Company"). The [North–South Rail Link](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North%E2%80%93South_Rail_Link "North–South Rail Link") is a proposed tunnel between North Station and South Station to allow through-running service.

The system consists of twelve lines – four of which have branches – radiating from [downtown Boston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Downtown_Boston "Downtown Boston"). Eight "southside" lines terminate at [South Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Station "South Station"), with four (Framingham/Worcester, Needham, Franklin/Foxboro, and Providence/Stoughton) also running through [Back Bay station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Back_Bay_station "Back Bay station"). Four "northside" lines terminate at [North Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Station "North Station"). The lines vary in length from the 9.2-mile (14.8 km) Fairmount Line to the 62.9-mile (101.2 km) Providence/Stoughton Line, with typical lengths in the 25–40-mile (40–64 km) range.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_Commuter_Rail#cite_note-bluebook-3) The system has 429 miles (690 km) of revenue trackage and covers roughly the eastern third of Massachusetts plus central Rhode Island.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_Commuter_Rail#cite_note-bluebook-3)[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_Commuter_Rail#cite_note-mbtaptc-4)
