An EMD FP10 locomotive with rented GO Transit coaches at South Station in 1979

As the MBTA assumed control of the commuter rail during the 1970s, it inherited various equipment from predecessor railroads.[\[112\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_Commuter_Rail#cite_note-railwayage-113) The 1976 purchase of B&M and Penn Central equipment included 94 [Budd Rail Diesel Cars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Budd_Rail_Diesel_Car "Budd Rail Diesel Car") (RDCs) – 86 from the B&M and eight from Penn Central – plus 116 Penn Central coaches and 25 Penn Central [E8](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EMD_E8 "EMD E8") and [GP9](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EMD_GP9 "EMD GP9") diesel locomotives.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_Commuter_Rail#cite_note-roster-14) Although the MBTA purchased some new equipment in 1978–1980, large locomotive and coach fleets were not purchased until the late 1980s, so the first decade of combined operations used a variety of secondhand equipment in addition to that acquired in 1976:[\[112\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_Commuter_Rail#cite_note-railwayage-113)[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_Commuter_Rail#cite_note-roster-14)

*   Four [ALCO PA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ALCO_PA "ALCO PA") locomotives leased from the [Delaware and Hudson Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delaware_and_Hudson_Railway "Delaware and Hudson Railway") in 1978[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_Commuter_Rail#cite_note-roster-14)
*   48 coaches leased from [GO Transit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GO_Transit "GO Transit") in 1978–1980. 51 coaches (some of which were in the previous group) were leased in 1984–85.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_Commuter_Rail#cite_note-roster-14)
*   19 [EMD GP7](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EMD_GP7 "EMD GP7") locomotives leased from the B&M in 1978–1982[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_Commuter_Rail#cite_note-roster-14)
*   24 RDCs acquired or leased from [MARC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MARC_Train "MARC Train"), [SEPTA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SEPTA_Regional_Rail "SEPTA Regional Rail"), and [New Jersey Transit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NJ_Transit_Rail_Operations "NJ Transit Rail Operations") between 1983 and 1987[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_Commuter_Rail#cite_note-roster-14)
*   11 EMD GP9 locomotives acquired from the [Burlington Northern Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington_Northern_Railroad "Burlington Northern Railroad") and [SEMTA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SEMTA "SEMTA") in 1983–1986[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_Commuter_Rail#cite_note-roster-14)
*   One [EMD SW9](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EMD_SW9 "EMD SW9") locomotive acquired from the [Seaboard Coast Line Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seaboard_Coast_Line_Railroad "Seaboard Coast Line Railroad") in 1984[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_Commuter_Rail#cite_note-roster-14)

Most of the secondhand and inherited equipment was retired between 1979 and 1989. 33 ex-B&M RDCs were converted to locomotive-hauled coaches (designated BTC-2 and CTC-2) in 1980 and 1982; they were retired by 1989. This left all MBTA service operated by locomotives and coaches purchased new by the MBTA.[\[112\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_Commuter_Rail#cite_note-railwayage-113)[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_Commuter_Rail#cite_note-roster-14) At several points since, the MBTA or its contract operator has temporarily leased locomotives when needed. Some passenger equipment acquired new by the MBTA has been retired:

*   18 [EMD F40PH](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EMD_F40PH "EMD F40PH") locomotives (1000–1017), built 1978–1980 and last ran in 2015[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_Commuter_Rail#cite_note-roster-14)
*   19 [EMD FP10](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EMD_FP10 "EMD FP10") locomotives (1100–1114 and 1150–1153), rebuilt 1979 from [Gulf, Mobile and Ohio Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf,_Mobile_and_Ohio_Railroad "Gulf, Mobile and Ohio Railroad") locomotives and last ran in 1991[\[112\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_Commuter_Rail#cite_note-railwayage-113)[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_Commuter_Rail#cite_note-roster-14)

The following improvement projects are actively being pursued by the MBTA and are at various stages of construction, planning, or funding.

### Regional Rail Modernization Program

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=MBTA_Commuter_Rail&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Regional Rail Modernization Program")\]

[![Image 36](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4f/Providence_Line_train_approaching_Canton_Junction%2C_April_2016.JPG/250px-Providence_Line_train_approaching_Canton_Junction%2C_April_2016.JPG)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Providence_Line_train_approaching_Canton_Junction,_April_2016.JPG)

A diesel MBTA train on the electrified Northeast Corridor

The Regional Rail Modernization Program is a phased initiative by the MBTA to transition the [commuter rail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commuter_rail "Commuter rail") system from diesel-powered, peak-oriented service to an [electrified](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Railway_electrification "Railway electrification") [regional rail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regional_rail "Regional rail") network with frequent all-day service. The program was formally initiated in early 2025 following several years of planning, with initial phases focused on near-term improvements to existing diesel operations.[\[113\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_Commuter_Rail#cite_note-114)

Regional rail concepts were first proposed in the late 2010s after the cancellation of the [Indigo Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indigo_Line "Indigo Line") project (a proposed [hybrid rail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hybrid_rail "Hybrid rail") network) in 2015.[\[114\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_Commuter_Rail#cite_note-115)[\[115\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_Commuter_Rail#cite_note-:0-116) Between 2018 and 2019, the MBTA conducted the _Rail Vision_ study to evaluate regional rail alternatives, drawing on domestic and international examples.[\[116\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_Commuter_Rail#cite_note-117)[\[117\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_Commuter_Rail#cite_note-118)[\[118\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_Commuter_Rail#cite_note-119)[\[119\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_Commuter_Rail#cite_note-120)[\[120\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_Commuter_Rail#cite_note-121)[\[121\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_Commuter_Rail#cite_note-122)[\[122\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_Commuter_Rail#cite_note-123) In 2019, the concept was formally endorsed by the now-defunct Fiscal and Management Control Board, and the MBTA engaged [Network Rail Consulting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Network_Rail "Network Rail") to assist with planning.[\[115\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_Commuter_Rail#cite_note-:0-116)

Despite formal endorsement by the Fiscal and Management Control Board, planning for regional rail stagnated into the early 2020s.[\[123\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_Commuter_Rail#cite_note-124)[\[124\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_Commuter_Rail#cite_note-draft2529cip-125) Several proposed electrification pilots were ultimately cancelled.[\[125\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_Commuter_Rail#cite_note-126)[\[126\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_Commuter_Rail#cite_note-127) By 2022, rising costs led the MBTA to consider [battery electric multiple units](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battery_electric_multiple_unit "Battery electric multiple unit") (BEMUs) with limited [catenary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Overhead_line "Overhead line") infrastructure for charging, as a cost-saving measure.[\[127\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_Commuter_Rail#cite_note-june2022electric-128)[\[128\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_Commuter_Rail#cite_note-129)[\[129\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_Commuter_Rail#cite_note-130)[\[130\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_Commuter_Rail#cite_note-131) By early 2024, a [public-private partnership](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public%E2%80%93private_partnership "Public–private partnership") model was also adopted as the preferred framework for delivering future regional rail projects.[\[131\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_Commuter_Rail#cite_note-132) In July 2024, the MBTA approved a $54 million pilot proposal from [Keolis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keolis "Keolis") to electrify the Fairmount Line using BEMUs, with 20-minute headways planned by 2028.[\[132\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_Commuter_Rail#cite_note-133)[\[124\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_Commuter_Rail#cite_note-draft2529cip-125)[\[133\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_Commuter_Rail#cite_note-134)[\[134\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_Commuter_Rail#cite_note-135)[\[135\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_Commuter_Rail#cite_note-136)[\[136\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_Commuter_Rail#cite_note-137) As of 2025, planned improvements to all other commuter rail lines are limited to diesel service upgrades—including new [turnback tracks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turnback_track "Turnback track"), track replacement, and increased service frequency—with electrification deferred to a long-term future phase.[\[137\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_Commuter_Rail#cite_note-138)[\[138\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_Commuter_Rail#cite_note-139)[\[139\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_Commuter_Rail#cite_note-140)

### Station renovations

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=MBTA_Commuter_Rail&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Station renovations")\]

[![Image 37](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2d/Outbound_train_passing_Natick_Center_station_construction_%282%29%2C_March_2022.JPG/250px-Outbound_train_passing_Natick_Center_station_construction_%282%29%2C_March_2022.JPG)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Outbound_train_passing_Natick_Center_station_construction_/(2/),_March_2022.JPG)

Reconstruction of Natick Center station in 2022

Several station renovations for [accessibility](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Accessibility "Accessibility"), expanded service, and/or repairs are under construction or planned:

*   Accessible platforms at [Natick Center station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natick_Center_station "Natick Center station") opened in July 2025, with some construction ongoing.[\[140\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_Commuter_Rail#cite_note-141)
*   A new [island platform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Island_platform "Island platform") at [Worcester Union Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Worcester_Union_Station "Worcester Union Station") was opened on July 1, 2024, with the project expected to be fully complete in August 2025.[\[141\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_Commuter_Rail#cite_note-142)[\[142\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_Commuter_Rail#cite_note-SWADec2024-143)
*   Design work for reconstruction of [South Attleboro station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Attleboro_station "South Attleboro station") for accessibility was completed in April 2022, though construction work has not been funded. The station was temporarily closed on February 26, 2021, due to structural deterioration; limited service resumed on May 20, 2024.[\[143\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_Commuter_Rail#cite_note-swanov2023-144)[\[144\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_Commuter_Rail#cite_note-145)[\[145\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_Commuter_Rail#cite_note-146)
*   Reconstruction of [Lynn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lynn_station "Lynn station") is planned. The station was temporarily closed in October 2022 due to structural deterioration; interim platforms opened in December 2023.[\[146\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_Commuter_Rail#cite_note-147)
*   Reconstruction of [Auburndale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auburndale_station_/(MBTA/) "Auburndale station (MBTA)"), [West Newton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Newton_station "West Newton station"), and [Newtonville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newtonville_station "Newtonville station") for accessibility and increased capacity are planned.[\[143\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_Commuter_Rail#cite_note-swanov2023-144) In November 2024, the state committed to the reconstruction of Newtonville station.[\[147\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_Commuter_Rail#cite_note-148)
*   In 2024, the MBTA tested a temporary freestanding accessible platform design at [Beverly Depot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beverly_Depot "Beverly Depot"). These platforms do not require alterations to the existing platforms, thus skirting federal rules requiring full accessibility renovations when stations are modified, and were intended to provide interim accessibility at lower cost pending full reconstruction.[\[148\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_Commuter_Rail#cite_note-may2024-149) Construction of interim platforms at four stations began in 2024 and was completed in 2025.[\[142\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_Commuter_Rail#cite_note-SWADec2024-143)[\[149\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_Commuter_Rail#cite_note-150)[\[150\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_Commuter_Rail#cite_note-151) Eight more stations are planned to receive the platforms; the second group will be [Concord](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concord_station_/(Massachusetts/) "Concord station (Massachusetts)"), [Endicott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endicott_station "Endicott station"), [Lincoln](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lincoln_station_/(MBTA/) "Lincoln station (MBTA)"), [Wakefield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wakefield_station_/(MBTA/) "Wakefield station (MBTA)"), and [Wyoming Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wyoming_Hill_station "Wyoming Hill station").[\[142\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_Commuter_Rail#cite_note-SWADec2024-143)
*   Reconstruction of [Foxboro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foxboro_station "Foxboro station") is planned for the [2026 World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_World_Cup "2026 World Cup").[\[151\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_Commuter_Rail#cite_note-152)

These projects stem from past expansion and improvement studies, as well as service proposals from various constituencies, but none have been advanced or approved by the MBTA.

Two extensions of existing lines have been studied in the 2020s:

*   Extension of the Middleborough/Lakeville Line to [Buzzards Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buzzards_Bay_station "Buzzards Bay station") or [Sagamore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sagamore_station "Sagamore station") (both in [Bourne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bourne,_Massachusetts "Bourne, Massachusetts")) to serve [Cape Cod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Cod "Cape Cod") was studied in 1997, and extension to Buzzards Bay was again studied in 2007.[\[152\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_Commuter_Rail#cite_note-153)[\[153\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_Commuter_Rail#cite_note-154) The extension was again proposed after the 2013 introduction of the CapeFLYER. The town of Bourne voted in 2015 to join the MBTA district.[\[154\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_Commuter_Rail#cite_note-155) MassDOT began planning a possible commuter rail trial service in October 2015.[\[155\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_Commuter_Rail#cite_note-rausch-156) The proposed service, which was to have shuttle trains between Bourne and [Middleborough/​Lakeville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lakeville_station "Lakeville station") operated by [Massachusetts Coastal Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Coastal_Railroad "Massachusetts Coastal Railroad"), was rejected by the MBTA Fiscal Management and Control Board in April 2016.[\[156\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_Commuter_Rail#cite_note-157) [Middleborough station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middleborough_station "Middleborough station"), which replaced Middleborough/Lakeville in 2025 when South Coast Rail service began, was built with space for a potential future platform for shuttle trains.[\[157\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_Commuter_Rail#cite_note-scr-dseir-158): 37  A 2021 study analyzed two alternatives for service to Buzzards Bay or [Bourne station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bourne_station "Bourne station"). Middleborough–Buzzards Bay shuttle service with 7 daily round trips was expected to have 1,710 total daily boardings, while Middleborough–Bourne service with 10 daily round trips (including two off-peak Boston–Bourne round trips) was expected to have 2,540 total daily boardings.[\[158\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_Commuter_Rail#cite_note-159)
*   Extension of the Lowell Line to [Manchester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_Station_/(Manchester,_New_Hampshire/) "Union Station (Manchester, New Hampshire)") and [Nashua, New Hampshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nashua,_New_Hampshire "Nashua, New Hampshire") has been proposed since the 1980–81 pilot service.[\[159\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_Commuter_Rail#cite_note-160) The extension has been a politically contentious issue at the state level in New Hampshire, with Democratic politicians supporting the service and Republican politicians opposing it.[\[160\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_Commuter_Rail#cite_note-nhbr-161) A 2014 alternatives analysis recommended several possible services, including commuter rail to Nashua or Manchester or [intercity rail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intercity_rail "Intercity rail") to Concord, for further evaluation.[\[161\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_Commuter_Rail#cite_note-162) Engineering and design work for commuter service to Manchester began in late 2020, and was completed in February 2023.[\[162\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_Commuter_Rail#cite_note-163)

### North–South Rail Link

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=MBTA_Commuter_Rail&action=edit&section=23 "Edit section: North–South Rail Link")\]

No direct connection exists between the two downtown commuter rail terminals; passengers must use the [MBTA subway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_subway "MBTA subway") or other modes to transfer between the two halves of the system. (For non-revenue transfers of equipment, the MBTA and Amtrak use the [Grand Junction Branch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Junction_Railroad_and_Depot_Company "Grand Junction Railroad and Depot Company").) The proposed [North–South Rail Link](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North%E2%80%93South_Rail_Link "North–South Rail Link") would add a new rail tunnel under downtown Boston to allow through-running service, with new underground stations at South Station, North Station, and possibly [a new Central Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aquarium_station_/(MBTA/)#Central_Station_proposal "Aquarium station (MBTA)"). A feasibility study was conducted in 2018.[\[187\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_Commuter_Rail#cite_note-188)

| | The **Kingston Line** is a [commuter rail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commuter_rail "Commuter rail") line of the [MBTA Commuter Rail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_Commuter_Rail "MBTA Commuter Rail") system in southeastern Massachusetts, United States. It runs 35.1 miles (56.5 km) southeast from [Boston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston "Boston") to [Kingston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston,_Massachusetts "Kingston, Massachusetts") with eight intermediate stops. [Plymouth station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plymouth_station_/(MBTA/) "Plymouth station (MBTA)"), which served as a second outer terminal, has been indefinitely closed since 2021. The line had 4,171 boardings per weekday in October 2022.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_Line#cite_note-oct2022ridership-1) The line originated as the [Old Colony Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Colony_Railroad#Old_Colony_Railroad_\(1844%E2%80%931854\) "Old Colony Railroad"), which opened between Boston and [Plymouth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plymouth,_Massachusetts "Plymouth, Massachusetts") in 1845. It became the primary rail route between Boston and southeastern Massachusetts, serving a number of branches that the Old Colony built and acquired. The Old Colony merged in 1854 to become the [Old Colony and Fall River Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Colony_and_Fall_River_Railroad "Old Colony and Fall River Railroad"), in 1863 to become the [Old Colony and Newport Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Colony_and_Newport_Railway "Old Colony and Newport Railway"), and in 1872 to become the [Old Colony Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Colony_Railroad "Old Colony Railroad"). It was leased by the [New York, New Haven and Hartford Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York,_New_Haven_and_Hartford_Railroad "New York, New Haven and Hartford Railroad") in 1893. Commuter service peaked in the early 20th century and began to decline in the 1910s. After two decades of attempts to end Old Colony Division service, the New Haven terminated it in 1959. Planning for the [Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Bay_Transportation_Authority "Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority") to restore service to Plymouth began in the 1980s. Construction began in 1993 and service began in 1997 as the **Plymouth/Kingston Line**.[\[a\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_Line#cite_note-name-2) It became the Kingston Line after the closure of Plymouth station. [![Image 93: A railway station with a high-level platform and one track](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/33/Kingston_Route_3_MBTA_station%2C_Kingston_MA.jpg/250px-Kingston_Route_3_MBTA_station%2C_Kingston_MA.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Kingston_Route_3_MBTA_station,_Kingston_MA.jpg) Kingston station is the line's southern terminus. The northern section of the line follows the [Middleborough Main Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middleborough_Main_Line "Middleborough Main Line") south through Boston, [Quincy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quincy,_Massachusetts "Quincy, Massachusetts"), and [Braintree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Braintree,_Massachusetts "Braintree, Massachusetts"). That section is shared with the [Fall River/New Bedford Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line "Fall River/New Bedford Line") and [Greenbush Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenbush_Line "Greenbush Line").[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_Line#cite_note-dseir-3): 47  At Braintree, the line switches to the **Plymouth Branch**, which continues southeast through [Weymouth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weymouth,_Massachusetts "Weymouth, Massachusetts"), [Abington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abington,_Massachusetts "Abington, Massachusetts"), [Whitman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whitman,_Massachusetts "Whitman, Massachusetts"), [Hanson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hanson,_Massachusetts "Hanson, Massachusetts"), [Halifax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halifax,_Massachusetts "Halifax, Massachusetts"), and [Kingston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston,_Massachusetts "Kingston, Massachusetts"). Intermediate stations are served at [JFK/UMass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JFK/UMass_station "JFK/UMass station"), [Quincy Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quincy_Center_station "Quincy Center station"), [Braintree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Braintree_station_/(MBTA/) "Braintree station (MBTA)"), [South Weymouth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Weymouth_station "South Weymouth station"), [Abington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abington_station "Abington station"), [Whitman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whitman_station "Whitman station"), and [Halifax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halifax_station_/(MBTA/) "Halifax station (MBTA)"). In Kingston, the short **Kingston Branch** splits from the Plymouth Branch and runs south to [Kingston station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_station_/(MBTA/) "Kingston station (MBTA)") and the [Kingston Layover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Massachusetts_Bay_Transportation_Authority_yards "List of Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority yards"). The Plymouth Branch continues southeast from the split to the currently-closed [Plymouth station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plymouth_station_/(MBTA/) "Plymouth station (MBTA)") in northern [Plymouth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plymouth,_Massachusetts "Plymouth, Massachusetts").[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_Line#cite_note-transitmatters-4): 11 [\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_Line#cite_note-executive-5): 2  The Plymouth Branch is single track with passing sidings, while the Kingston Branch is mostly double-tracked. The portion of the Middleborough Main Line used by the Kingston Line has a mixture of single and double track.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_Line#cite_note-transitmatters-4): 11 [\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_Line#cite_note-trackchart-6) Like the rest of the MBTA Commuter Rail system, the Kingston Line operates using [push-pull trains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Push-pull_train "Push-pull train") with diesel locomotives.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_Line#cite_note-executive-5): 5  Maximum speeds are between 60–80 miles per hour (97–129 km/h) south of Braintree and 40–60 miles per hour (64–97 km/h) to the north.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_Line#cite_note-transitmatters-4): 12  As of October 2025, the line has 13 inbound and 12 outbound trips on weekdays and nine round trips on weekdays. Most trips operate the full length of the line, with running times typically around 60 minutes. The last trips in each direction, plus the first weekday inbound trip, only operate between Braintree and Kingston. Trains always serve all stops except for JFK/UMass, which is only served at weekday peak hours in the peak direction.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_Line#cite_note-7) All stations are [accessible](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Accessible "Accessible") with full-length high-level platforms.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_Line#cite_note-transitmatters-4): 10 #### Old Colony Railroad \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kingston_Line&action=edit§ion=4 "Edit section: Old Colony Railroad")\] [![Image 94: See caption.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b6/OC1893.jpg/250px-OC1893.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:OC1893.jpg) Map of the Old Colony Railroad in 1893 The [Old Colony Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Colony_Railroad#Old_Colony_Railroad_\(1844%E2%80%931854\) "Old Colony Railroad") opened between [South Boston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broadway_station_/(MBTA/)#History "Broadway station (MBTA)") and Plymouth on November 10, 1845.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_Line#cite_note-150years-8): 95  A short extension into Boston proper opened in March 1846.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_Line#cite_note-secondsection-9): 6  As the only rail line east of the [Blue Hills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Hills_Reservation "Blue Hills Reservation"), the Old Colony became the primary rail route between Boston and southeastern Massachusetts. The Old Colony built or acquired a number of other lines, all of which used the Old Colony mainline to access Boston. The [Fall River Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River_Railroad_/(1846/) "Fall River Railroad (1846)") (1846), [Milton Branch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorchester_and_Milton_Branch_Railroad "Dorchester and Milton Branch Railroad") (1847), [South Shore Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Shore_Railroad "South Shore Railroad") (1849), [Dighton and Somerset Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dighton_and_Somerset_Railroad "Dighton and Somerset Railroad") (1866), and [Granite Branch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granite_Railway "Granite Railway") (1871) all joined the mainline between [South Braintree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Braintree_station_/(MBTA/)#History "Braintree station (MBTA)") and Boston. The [Hanover Branch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hanover_Branch_Railroad "Hanover Branch Railroad") (1868) joined at [North Abington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Abington_station "North Abington station"), while the [Bridgewater Branch](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bridgewater_Branch&action=edit&redlink=1 "Bridgewater Branch (page does not exist)") (1847) joined at Whitman.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_Line#cite_note-sne-10): 376 [\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_Line#cite_note-150years-8): 95 The mainline was double-tracked between Boston and South Braintree in 1848 to serve the growing traffic.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_Line#cite_note-150years-8): 95  Schedules were suitable for commuting from as far south as South Braintree by 1847; commuter service to Plymouth was intermittent until around 1860 and consistent thereafter. Some [short turn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Short_turn "Short turn") trains terminated at Whitman after 1860.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_Line#cite_note-150years-8): 95  The Old Colony merged in 1854 to become the [Old Colony and Fall River Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Colony_and_Fall_River_Railroad "Old Colony and Fall River Railroad"), in 1863 to become the [Old Colony and Newport Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Colony_and_Newport_Railway "Old Colony and Newport Railway"), and in 1872 to become the Old Colony Railroad.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_Line#cite_note-sne-10): 376  The [Plymouth and Vineyard Sound Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plymouth_and_Vineyard_Sound_Railroad "Plymouth and Vineyard Sound Railroad"), an extension beyond Plymouth to Cape Cod, was proposed in the 1860s, but only the Cape Cod section between [Buzzards Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buzzards_Bay_station "Buzzards Bay station") and [Woods Hole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woods_Hole_station "Woods Hole station") was built.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_Line#cite_note-11) Major wrecks took place on the mainline [at Wollaston in 1878](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wollaston_disaster "Wollaston disaster") and [at Quincy in 1890](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1890_Quincy_train_wreck "1890 Quincy train wreck").[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_Line#cite_note-sne-10): 379  To reduce congestion on the busy mainline and make trains faster, the Old Colony used a practice called [flying switches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flying_switch "Flying switch"). The rear coaches of moving trains were disconnected at speed near junctions and brought to a halt to serve as branchline trains, while the rest of the train continued without stopping. The practice was ended after an 1883 incident at Neponset.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_Line#cite_note-secondsection-9): 7  After Old Colony acquired the [Boston and Providence Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_and_Providence_Railroad "Boston and Providence Railroad") in 1888, some trains were routed via the [Stoughton Branch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stoughton_Branch "Stoughton Branch") to reduce mainline congestion.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_Line#cite_note-sne-10): 182 [\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_Line#cite_note-secondsection-9): 7 [![Image 95: A postcard of a passenger train with a steam locomotive at a two-story wooden station](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7d/Abington_station_1910_postcard.jpg/250px-Abington_station_1910_postcard.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Abington_station_1910_postcard.jpg) Abington station around 1910 The [New York, New Haven and Hartford Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York,_New_Haven_and_Hartford_Railroad "New York, New Haven and Hartford Railroad") leased the Old Colony in 1893.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_Line#cite_note-sne-10): 393  Passenger service on the Old Colony Division was at its peak from around 1898 to 1914. In 1898, daily inbound service to Boston included seven trains from Plymouth and five from Whitman plus some through trains from the Bridgewater and Hanover branches. Six South Shore trains used the line between Plymouth and Kingston.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_Line#cite_note-150years-8): 96  The mainline was relocated between South Boston and [Crescent Avenue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JFK/UMass_station#History "JFK/UMass station") in 1897–1898 to eliminate grade crossings in preparation for the 1899 opening of [South Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Station "South Station").[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_Line#cite_note-secondsection-9): 6–7  The line was quadruple-tracked from South Boston to [Savin Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Savin_Hill_station "Savin Hill station") in 1901–02, to Neponset in 1911–12, and to [Atlantic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Quincy_station#History "North Quincy station") in 1913, including grade crossing eliminations.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_Line#cite_note-secondsection-9): 7  Double track was added between Kingston and Plymouth in 1900 and between South Braintree and Whitman in 1907.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_Line#cite_note-150years-8): 95 During World War I, a short branch was built from the mainline to the [Victory Destroyer Plant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victory_Destroyer_Plant "Victory Destroyer Plant") to carry materials and workers.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_Line#cite_note-12) Systemwide passenger service levels began to decline during the war when freight was given priority, and continued to decline thereafter.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_Line#cite_note-150years-8): 96  By 1924, inbound service included six trains from Plymouth, three from Whitman, two from the Bridgewater Branch, and four from Hanover.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_Line#cite_note-13) Bridgewater Branch service ended in urban Metropolitan Transit Authority into the surrounding suburbs. The MBTA was intended to subsidize commuter rail service – and to replace much of it with rapid transit extensions.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_Line#cite_note-150years-8): 13 The MBTA's first such project was a branch of the [Red Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Line_/(MBTA/) "Red Line (MBTA)") (Cambridge–Dorchester Line) following the Old Colony alignment to Braintree.[\[b\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_Line#cite_note-28) In November 1965, the MBTA purchased the Old Colony main line between Boston and South Braintree from the New Haven.[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_Line#cite_note-29)[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_Line#cite_note-clarke-25): 22  The Red Line opened to [Quincy Center station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quincy_Center_station "Quincy Center station") in September 1971 and [Braintree station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Braintree_station_/(MBTA/) "Braintree station (MBTA)") in South Braintree in March 1980.[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_Line#cite_note-netransit-30)[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_Line#cite_note-problem3-22): 36  Within Boston, a single freight track paralleled the new tracks. The resulting cancellation of the [Southwest Expressway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southwest_Corridor_/(Massachusetts/)#Highway_proposal "Southwest Corridor (Massachusetts)") by the [Boston Transportation Planning Review](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Transportation_Planning_Review "Boston Transportation Planning Review") meant the already-overcrowded Southeast Expressway would continue to be the only highway into Boston from the south.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_Line#cite_note-problem3-22): 36 [\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_Line#cite_note-150years-8): 16  In January 1973, the MBTA acquired most of Penn Central's suburban lines around Boston, including the Plymouth line.[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_Line#cite_note-31)[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_Line#cite_note-32)[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_Line#cite_note-33) Freight service continued to operate on the line, though the segment from North Plymouth to Plymouth was out of service by the late 1970s.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_Line#cite_note-sne-10): 380 [![Image 97: View of a 2-track railway line from above a tunnel portal](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/60/Kingston_Branch_tunnel_portal%2C_June_2017.JPG/250px-Kingston_Branch_tunnel_portal%2C_June_2017.JPG)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Kingston_Branch_tunnel_portal,_June_2017.JPG) The northern end of the Kingston Branch tunnel under Route 3 In 1984, a state-directed MBTA study found that restoration of commuter rail service on the former Old Colony lines would be feasible.[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_Line#cite_note-ES-34): 4  A Draft Environmental Impact Statement for restoration of service on the Middleborough, Plymouth, and Greenbush lines was released in May 1990. It called for the terminal to be in [North Plymouth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Plymouth,_Massachusetts "North Plymouth, Massachusetts") south of [Cordage Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plymouth_Cordage_Company "Plymouth Cordage Company"), with Kingston/Route 3 station next to the [Route 3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Route_3 "Massachusetts Route 3") expressway. A layover yard would have been built in Cordage Park.[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_Line#cite_note-35) In 1991, the state agreed to build a set of transit projects as part of an agreement with the [Conservation Law Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservation_Law_Foundation "Conservation Law Foundation") (CLF), which had threatened a lawsuit over auto emissions from the Central Artery/Tunnel Project ([Big Dig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Dig "Big Dig")). Among these projects was the "Old Colony Commuter Rail Line Extension", to be complete by the end of 1996.[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_Line#cite_note-1991agreement-36)[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_Line#cite_note-37)[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_Line#cite_note-38) The terminal plans became the subject of local controversy. The owner of both the proposed station sites objected to both; he planned to develop the Plymouth station site with residential buildings, and did not wish to sell the Kingston station site where he owned a beer distribution warehouse. The Cordage Park owners objected to the layover yard on their property but wanted the station moved there.[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_Line#cite_note-39) In April 1991, the MBTA announced a new plan. A new rail spur would be built along Route 3 with a Kingston station and layover yard in a former sand and gravel lot being redeveloped as an industrial park. The Plymouth station would be built at Cordage Park with no layover yard; it would only have off-peak and weekend service, with peak-hour service only running to Kingston.[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_Line#cite_note-40)[\[c\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_Line#cite_note-42) The Final Environmental Impact Statement for the Middleborough and Plymouth lines – often called the "Old Colony Lines" – was released in 1992.[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_Line#cite_note-43)[\[d\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_Line#cite_note-44) It incorporated the terminal changes announced in 1991. It also moved the Abington station from [North Abington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Abington_station "North Abington station") to [a site near the town center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abington_station "Abington station") and removed a potential stop in downtown Kingston.[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_Line#cite_note-ES-34): 31 Construction of the $560 million project began in 1993, with service then expected to begin in late 1996.[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_Line#cite_note-45) Which stations to include on the shared mainline between Braintree and Boston also proved controversial. [![Image 1](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/64/MBTA.svg/250px-MBTA.svg.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:MBTA.svg)

MBTA "lollipop" logo, designed by [Tom Geismar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Geismar "Tom Geismar") of [CambridgeSeven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CambridgeSeven "CambridgeSeven") architects in the 1960s. The group decided to nickname the service "The T" and modelled the logo after Stockholm's _[Tunnelbana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tunnelbana "Tunnelbana")_.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-Bloomberg-1)

[![Image 2](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/ba/MBTA_1105_at_Bradford%2C_circa_1979.jpg/250px-MBTA_1105_at_Bradford%2C_circa_1979.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:MBTA_1105_at_Bradford,_circa_1979.jpg)

An MBTA train, c. 1979

[![Image 3](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f8/MBTA_route_245_bus%2C_circa_1972.jpg/250px-MBTA_route_245_bus%2C_circa_1972.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:MBTA_route_245_bus,_circa_1972.jpg)

An MBTA bus, c. 1972

The history of the [Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Bay_Transportation_Authority "Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority") (MBTA) and its predecessors spans two centuries, starting with one of the oldest railroads in the United States. Development of mass transportation both followed existing economic and population patterns, and helped shape those patterns.

Privately owned mass transit in the Boston area evolved from the colonial period into the early 1900s, including ferries, steamships, steam commuter railroads, horse and electric streetcars, elevated railways, and subways. Many streetcar lines were consolidated into the [West End Street Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_End_Street_Railway "West End Street Railway") in 1887. This was merged into the [Boston Elevated Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Elevated_Railway "Boston Elevated Railway") in 1897, which that same year opened the first subway in the United States (the [Tremont Street subway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tremont_Street_subway "Tremont Street subway")). Subway construction was funded by city taxpayers, and overseen by the new Boston Transit Commission. As automobiles started causing financial problems for mass transit operators, the MTA took over the BER in 1947 and began replacing inner commuter rail service with rapid transit expansions. The MTA started running ferry services in 1963. The MBTA replaced the MTA in 1964, expanding the service area to fully include the area's commuter rail services, all of which had to be taken over by the government or discontinued for financial reasons. [Paratransit services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ride_/(MBTA/) "The Ride (MBTA)") began in 1977.

Except for the [Mattapan Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mattapan_Line "Mattapan Line") and some portions of the [Green Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Line_/(MBTA/) "Green Line (MBTA)"), all streetcars were replaced by buses. The MBTA benefitted from a political turn away from highway construction in the 1970s, which resulted in relocation of part of the Orange Line. In the following decades, demand for mass transit services increased as the population migration out of the urban core toward the car-centric suburbs reversed, and overall population kept increasing.

The agency continued expanding and reactivating commuter rail services, and expanding rapid transit into the late 20th and early 21st century. The [Big Dig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Dig "Big Dig") (1991-2006) resulted in the creation of the Silver Line subway-busline and other promised expansions to mitigate the increased pollution caused by increased highway capacity (required after a [Clean Air Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clean_Air_Act_/(United_States/) "Clean Air Act (United States)") lawsuit by the [Conservation Law Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservation_Law_Foundation "Conservation Law Foundation")). In 2000, the state changed the MBTA financing mechanism from habitually paying expenses in arrears to getting a fixed budget: 1% of state retail sales (out of a total 5% statewide sales tax at the time) plus assessments from cities and towns in the service area. Partly due to an increase in [ecommerce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ecommerce "Ecommerce"), sales tax revenues were lower than expected, and because debt service for the Big Dig transit projects had been allocated to the MBTA, the agency experienced financial problems that required occasional supplemental state funding. It became a division of the newly consolidated [MassDOT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MassDOT "MassDOT") in 2009. During the term of Governor [Charlie Baker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlie_Baker "Charlie Baker") (2015-2023), deferred subway system maintenance from the period of austerity became problematic. A 2015 snowstorm shut down two subway lines, resulting in temporary appointment of a Fiscal and Management Control Board. During the recovery from the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic"), an accumulation of high-profile safety incidents resulted in a [Federal Transit Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Transit_Administration "Federal Transit Administration") investigation in 2022, and sudden safety-related service cuts.

Mass transit in [Boston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston "Boston"), [Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts "Massachusetts") began as a family-owned and operated ferry about the [time of the founding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston#Colonial "Boston") of Boston, in around 1630.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-2) Ground transportation started in Boston with a private stagecoach operation in 1793.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-3)

Boston and Maine Railroad lines are colored red, New York Central Railroad lines green, New York, New Haven and Hartford Railroad lines blue, and the Boston, Revere Beach and Lynn Railroad black.")

The [steam locomotive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steam_locomotive "Steam locomotive") became practical for mass transportation in the 1810s and came to the United States in the 1820s. Three railroads were built from Boston to other industrial cities in 1834–35: the [Boston and Lowell Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_and_Lowell_Railroad "Boston and Lowell Railroad"), [Boston and Worcester Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_and_Worcester_Railroad "Boston and Worcester Railroad"), and [Boston and Providence Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_and_Providence_Railroad "Boston and Providence Railroad"). There were soon eight intercity mainlines and numerous branches radiating from Boston. They were consolidated under three railroads in the last decades of the 19th century. Cuts from the 1910s to the 1950s ended service on many branches, but seven mainlines and several branches still had passenger service when the MBTA was formed in 1964.

### Boston and Maine Railroad

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_the_MBTA&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Boston and Maine Railroad")\]

Four of the current lines were part of the [Boston and Maine Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_and_Maine_Railroad "Boston and Maine Railroad") (B&M):

*   The [Newburyport/Rockport Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newburyport/Rockport_Line "Newburyport/Rockport Line") descends from the [Eastern Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Railroad "Eastern Railroad"), which opened from [East Boston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Boston "East Boston") to [Salem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salem_station_/(MBTA/) "Salem station (MBTA)") in 1838. It was extended to [Ipswich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ipswich_station_/(MBTA/) "Ipswich station (MBTA)") in 1839, to [Newburyport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newburyport_station "Newburyport station") in 1840, and eventually to [Portland, Maine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portland,_Maine "Portland, Maine") in 1842.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-sne-4): 314  The entry into Boston was built in 1854.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-sne-4): 315  The Gloucester Branch was built from [Beverly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beverly_Depot "Beverly Depot") to [Gloucester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gloucester_station_/(MBTA/) "Gloucester station (MBTA)") in 1847 and to [Rockport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rockport_station "Rockport station") in 1861.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-sne-4): 322  After a decades-long rivalry, the BM leased the Eastern in 1884. Passenger service on the Eastern Route mainline was cut back to Newburyport in 1965.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-sne-4): 316 
*   The [Haverhill Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haverhill_Line "Haverhill Line") descends from the [Andover and Wilmington Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andover_and_Wilmington_Railroad "Andover and Wilmington Railroad"), which opened from [Wilmington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilmington_station_/(MBTA/) "Wilmington station (MBTA)") to [Andover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andover_station_/(MBTA/) "Andover station (MBTA)") in 1836. It was extended to [Bradford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bradford_station "Bradford station") in 1837, to [Exeter, New Hampshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exeter,_New_Hampshire "Exeter, New Hampshire"), in 1840, and to Portland in 1843. A cutoff between Wilmington Junction and Boston was built in 1845, giving the B&M its own route into Boston. The Western Route became the spine of the B&M system. Passenger service was cut back to [Dover, New Hampshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dover,_New_Hampshire "Dover, New Hampshire"), in 1965 and to [Haverhill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haverhill_station_/(Massachusetts/) "Haverhill station (Massachusetts)") in 1967.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-sne-4): 291–294 
*   The [Lowell Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lowell_Line "Lowell Line") descends from the [Boston and Lowell Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_and_Lowell_Railroad "Boston and Lowell Railroad") (B&L), which opened in 1835.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-sne-4): 285  It was extended northwards by the [Nashua and Lowell Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nashua_and_Lowell_Railroad "Nashua and Lowell Railroad") in 1838 and the [Concord Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concord_Railroad "Concord Railroad") in 1842; both were later leased by the B&L.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-sne-4): 272  The B&M leased the B&L in 1887.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-sne-4): 286  Passenger service was cut back to [Lowell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lowell_station "Lowell station") in 1967.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-sne-4): 273 
*   The [Fitchburg Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fitchburg_Line "Fitchburg Line") descends from the [Fitchburg Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fitchburg_Railroad "Fitchburg Railroad"), which opened in phases from [West Cambridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Cambridge_/(neighborhood/) "West Cambridge (neighborhood)") to [Fitchburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fitchburg_Intermodal_Transportation_Center "Fitchburg Intermodal Transportation Center") in 1843–1845. It acquired the previously-built Charlestown Railroad, which ran between West Cambridge and [Charlestown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlestown,_Boston "Charlestown, Boston"), in 1844. A short extension into Boston opened in 1848.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-sne-4): 248  The [Vermont and Massachusetts Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vermont_and_Massachusetts_Railroad "Vermont and Massachusetts Railroad") was extended west to [Millers Falls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Millers_Falls,_Massachusetts "Millers Falls, Massachusetts") and north to [Brattleboro, Vermont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brattleboro,_Vermont "Brattleboro, Vermont"), in 1851, and west from Millers Falls to [Troy, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Troy,_New_York "Troy, New York"), in 1876 via the [Hoosac Tunnel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoosac_Tunnel "Hoosac Tunnel").[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-sne-4): 199, 201  The B&M leased the Fitchburg in 1900. Passenger service was cut back to Fitchburg in 1960.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-sne-4): 202 

The B&M system also included three lines closed during the MBTA era – the [Woburn Branch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woburn_Branch_Railroad "Woburn Branch Railroad") (1981), [Lexington Branch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lexington_Branch "Lexington Branch") (1977), and [Central Massachusetts Branch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Massachusetts_Branch "Central Massachusetts Branch") (1971) – and numerous lines closed prior to 1964.

### New York Central Railroad

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_the_MBTA&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: New York Central Railroad")\]

One current line was part of the [New York Central Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Central_Railroad "New York Central Railroad"), which merged into the [Penn Central Transportation Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penn_Central_Transportation_Company "Penn Central Transportation Company") in 1968:

*   The [Boston and Worcester Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_and_Worcester_Railroad "Boston and Worcester Railroad") opened from Boston to [Worcester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_Station_/(Worcester,_Massachusetts/) "Union Station (Worcester, Massachusetts)") in stages in 1834–35.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-sne-4): 342  The [Western Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Railroad_/(Massachusetts/) "Western Railroad (Massachusetts)") opened in stages from Worcester to [Albany, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albany,_New_York "Albany, New York"), in 1839–1841.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-sne-4): 190  The two railroads merged in 1867 as the [Boston and Albany Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_and_Albany_Railroad "Boston and Albany Railroad") (B&A), which was acquired by the New York Central in 1900.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-sne-4): 342 

Several B&A branch lines closed prior to 1964. The [Highland branch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Highland_branch "Highland branch") was closed in 1958 for conversion to a streetcar line, now the [Green Line D branch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Line_D_branch "Green Line D branch"). The freight-only [Grand Junction Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Junction_Railroad "Grand Junction Railroad"), formerly owned by the B&A, is used by the MBTA for equipment moves.

### New York, New Haven and Hartford Railroad

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_the_MBTA&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: New York, New Haven and Hartford Railroad")\]

Seven of the current lines were part of the [New York, New Haven and Hartford Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York,_New_Haven_and_Hartford_Railroad "New York, New Haven and Hartford Railroad"), which merged into Penn Central in 1969. Four were operated when the MBTA was formed:

*   The [Providence/Stoughton Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Providence/Stoughton_Line "Providence/Stoughton Line") descends from the [Boston and Providence Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_and_Providence_Railroad "Boston and Providence Railroad") (B&P), which opened between Boston and [Providence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_Station_/(Providence,_Rhode_Island/) "Union Station (Providence, Rhode Island)") in 1834–35.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-sne-4): 177  The [New York, Providence and Boston Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York,_Providence_and_Boston_Railroad "New York, Providence and Boston Railroad") (NYP&B) opened southwest from Providence in 1837, with a short connector into downtown Providence opened in 1848.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-sne-4): 147  The Stoughton Branch opened from [Canton Junction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canton_Junction_station "Canton Junction station") to [Stoughton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stoughton_station "Stoughton station") in 1845.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-sne-4): 181  A new routing between [Attleboro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attleboro,_Massachusetts "Attleboro, Massachusetts") and Providence opened in 1847.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-sne-4): 177  The [Old Colony Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Colony_Railroad "Old Colony Railroad") acquired the B&P in 1888. The New Haven acquired an NYP&B successor in 1892 and the Old Colony in 1893, using the NYP&B and the B&P as part of its New York–Boston mainline (now part of the [Northeast Corridor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northeast_Corridor "Northeast Corridor")).[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-sne-4): 178 
*   The [Fairmount Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fairmount_Line "Fairmount Line") descends from the [Midland Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midland_Railroad_/(Massachusetts/) "Midland Railroad (Massachusetts)"), which opened from Boston to [Islington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islington_station_/(MBTA/) "Islington station (MBTA)") via [Readville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Readville_station "Readville station") in 1855. It operated intermittently under several owners including the [Boston and New York Central Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_and_New_York_Central_Railroad "Boston and New York Central Railroad") and [Boston, Hartford and Erie Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston,_Hartford_and_Erie_Railroad "Boston, Hartford and Erie Railroad") until resuming full operation in 1867. The Boston, Hartford and Erie Railroad became part of the [New York and New England Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_and_New_England_Railroad "New York and New England Railroad") (NY&NE) in 1875. The New Haven acquired an NY&NE descendant in 1898 and rerouted through trains onto the BP north of Readville. Boston–Readville service ended in 1944 and did not resume until the MBTA era.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-sne-4): 361–363 
*   The [Franklin/Foxboro Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franklin/Foxboro_Line "Franklin/Foxboro Line") descends from the [Norfolk County Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norfolk_County_Railroad "Norfolk County Railroad"), which opened between [Dedham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedham_station "Dedham station") (on the B&P [Dedham Branch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedham_Branch "Dedham Branch")) and [Blackstone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blackstone,_Rhode_Island "Blackstone, Rhode Island") in 1849. It became part of the Boston and New York Central Railroad in 1853 and used the Midland Railroad (when operating) as its Boston entry after 1855. After several short-term operators, it became part of the Boston, Hartford and Erie Railroad in 1867. The New Haven cut back service to [Franklin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franklin_station_/(Massachusetts/) "Franklin station (Massachusetts)") in 1966. The Franklin–[Forge Park/495](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forge_Park/495_station "Forge Park/495 station") segment of the current line originated in 1882 as part of the [Milford and Woonsocket Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milford_and_Woonsocket_Railroad "Milford and Woonsocket Railroad"), which was leased by the NY&NE in 1887. Passenger service was intermittent after 1920 and was discontinued in 1940; it did not resume until the MBTA era.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-sne-4): 372  The [Walpole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_Station_/(Walpole,_Massachusetts/) "Union Station (Walpole, Massachusetts)")–[Foxboro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foxboro_station "Foxboro station") segment of the current line opened as part of the [Mansfield and Framingham Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mansfield_and_Framingham_Railroad "Mansfield and Framingham Railroad") in 1870 and became part of the Old Colony in 1879. Passenger service was discontinued in 1933 and did not resume until the MBTA era.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-sne-4): 374–375 
*   The [Needham Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Needham_Line "Needham Line") descends from two originally-unrelated branch lines. The B&P opened its West Roxbury Branch between [Forest Hills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forest_Hills_station_/(MBTA/) "Forest Hills station (MBTA)") and [Readville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Readville_station "Readville station") via [West Roxbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Roxbury_station "West Roxbury station") in 1849.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-sne-4): 180  The [Charles River Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_River_Railroad "Charles River Railroad") opened from [Newton Highlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newton_Highlands_station "Newton Highlands station") to [Needham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Needham_Center_station "Needham Center station") in 1853, using the Highand branch to reach Boston. It was extended to [Woonsocket, Rhode Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woonsocket,_Rhode_Island "Woonsocket, Rhode Island"), in 1861–1863 and became part of the Boston, Hartford and Erie Railroad in 1865.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-sne-4): 353  The New Haven opened a cutoff from [Needham Junction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Needham_Junction_station "Needham Junction station") to West Roxbury in 1906.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-sne-4): 353  Service north of [Needham Heights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Needham_Heights_station "Needham Heights station") ended in 1932. Service south of Needham Junction (the [Millis Branch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Millis_Branch "Millis Branch")) ended in 1967.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-sne-4): 351 

The New Haven ended all service on the Old Colony Division – the former [Old Colony Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Colony_Railroad "Old Colony Railroad") lines that were not part of the B&P – prior to formation of the MBTA. Service to [Fall River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River,_Massachusetts "Fall River, Massachusetts"), [New Bedford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Bedford,_Massachusetts "New Bedford, Massachusetts"), and [Taunton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taunton,_Massachusetts "Taunton, Massachusetts") via [Stoughton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stoughton_station "Stoughton station") ended in 1958. Service via [Quincy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quincy,_Massachusetts "Quincy, Massachusetts") ended in 1959, including three lines that were reactivated by the MBTA:

*   The [Kingston Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_Line "Kingston Line") descends from the [original Old Colony Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Colony_Railroad#Old_Colony_Railroad_\(1844%E2%80%931854\) "Old Colony Railroad"), which opened from Boston to [Plymouth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plymouth,_Massachusetts "Plymouth, Massachusetts") in 1845. It underwent several mergers, again becoming the Old Colony Railroad in 1872.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-sne-4): 378 
*   The [Middleborough/Lakeville Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middleborough/Lakeville_Line "Middleborough/Lakeville Line") descends from the [Fall River Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River_Railroad_/(1846/) "Fall River Railroad (1846)"), which opened from [South Braintree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Braintree_station_/(MBTA/)#History "Braintree station (MBTA)") to Fall River in 1846. It merged with the Old Colony in 1854. Passenger service between [Middleborough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middleborough_station "Middleborough station") and [Myricks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Myricks,_Massachusetts "Myricks, Massachusetts") in 1931 and south of Myricks in 1958.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-sne-4): 401  The segments opening as part of [South Coast Rail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail "South Coast Rail") include the East Taunton–New Bedford portion of the [New Bedford and Taunton Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Bedford_and_Taunton_Railroad "New Bedford and Taunton Railroad") (opened 1840, acquired by the Old Colony in 1879, passenger service ended 1958), the [Middleborough and Taunton Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middleborough_and_Taunton_Railroad "Middleborough and Taunton Railroad") (opened 1856, acquired by the Old Colony in 1879, passenger service ended 1927), and the Myricks–Fall River portion of the Fall River Railroad.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-sne-4): 398 
*   The [Greenbush Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenbush_Line "Greenbush Line") descends from the [South Shore Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Shore_Railroad "South Shore Railroad"), which opened from [Braintree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Braintree_station_/(MBTA/)#History "Braintree station (MBTA)") to [Cohasset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cohasset_station "Cohasset station") in 1849.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-sne-4): 384  The Duxbury and Cohasset Railroad extended the line to [South Duxbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Duxbury,_Massachusetts "South Duxbury, Massachusetts") in 1871 and [Kingston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_station_/(Rhode_Island/) "Kingston station (Rhode Island)") in 1874. The Old Colony acquired the two lines in 1877 and 1878.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-sne-4): 385  Passenger service south of [Greenbush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenbush_station "Greenbush station") ended in 1939.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-sne-4): 387 

Two New Haven lines closed in 1967 – the [Dedham Branch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedham_Branch "Dedham Branch") and the [Millis Branch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Millis_Branch "Millis Branch"). A number of other branches, particularly on the Old Colony Division, closed prior to the MBTA era. The [Shawmut Branch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shawmut_Branch_Railroad "Shawmut Branch Railroad") and part of the [Milton Branch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorchester_and_Milton_Branch_Railroad "Dorchester and Milton Branch Railroad") were converted to a streetcar line and rapid transit extension (now the [Mattapan Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mattapan_Line "Mattapan Line") and part of the [Red Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Line_/(MBTA/) "Red Line (MBTA)")) in 1926–1929.

### Boston, Revere Beach and Lynn Railroad

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_the_MBTA&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Boston, Revere Beach and Lynn Railroad")\]

The [Boston, Revere Beach and Lynn Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston,_Revere_Beach_and_Lynn_Railroad "Boston, Revere Beach and Lynn Railroad") opened from East Boston to [Lynn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lynn,_Massachusetts "Lynn, Massachusetts") in 1874. It was a [narrow-gauge railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Narrow-gauge_railroad "Narrow-gauge railroad") that never extended beyond Lynn or interchanged freight with other railroads, depending on short-distance passenger traffic. The line was electrified in 1928 with frequent commuter service. All service ended in 1940. A portion of the right-of-way in East Boston and [Revere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Revere,_Massachusetts "Revere, Massachusetts") was converted to a rapid transit extension – now part of the [Blue Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Line_/(MBTA/) "Blue Line (MBTA)") – in the 1950s.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-sne-4): 329–331

[![Image 5](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e9/1885_West_End_Street_Railway_map.png/250px-1885_West_End_Street_Railway_map.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:1885_West_End_Street_Railway_map.png)

Planned West End Street Railway system, 1885; consolidation of these lines was complete by 1887. See also [Boston horse railroads map.jpg 1880 horse railway map](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Image:1880).

The [Cambridge Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambridge_Railroad "Cambridge Railroad") was the first [streetcar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tram "Tram") company in Massachusetts. It was chartered in 1853 to connect the [West End of Boston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_End,_Boston,_Massachusetts "West End, Boston, Massachusetts") to [Central Square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Square_/(Cambridge/) "Central Square (Cambridge)") and [Harvard Square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_Square "Harvard Square") in [Cambridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambridge,_Massachusetts "Cambridge, Massachusetts") via the West End Bridge. (The bridge was replaced by the current [Longfellow Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Longfellow_Bridge "Longfellow Bridge") in early August 1906). This is the same route followed by today's [Red Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Line_/(MBTA/) "Red Line (MBTA)") subway, but on the surface street network. Using horse-drawn streetcars, the Cambridge Railroad started running on March 26, 1856. Another streetcar company, the [Dorchester Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorchester_Railroad "Dorchester Railroad"), was chartered in 1854. Over 20 streetcar lines were laid down throughout the Boston area by these and other competing companies.

In order to regulate fares and reduce competition, the General Court of Massachusetts passed the West End Consolidation Act to consolidate the rail line operations.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-5) This created the [West End Street Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_End_Street_Railway "West End Street Railway") in 1885. The company consolidated ownership of existing streetcar lines in Boston and the inner suburbs and began converting the animal-drawn vehicles to electric propulsion. In 1888, a [blizzard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blizzard "Blizzard") hit the [Northeastern United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northeastern_United_States "Northeastern United States") called the [Great Blizzard of 1888](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Blizzard_of_1888 "Great Blizzard of 1888"), creating rail and streetcar disturbances in [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City"), [Philadelphia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia "Philadelphia"), and other northeastern cities like [Boston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston "Boston"). The first electric trolleys ran in 1889, and the last [horsecar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horsecar "Horsecar") went out of service around 1900.

In the late 19th century and early 20th century, two other streetcar companies gained consolidated ownership of many smaller lines. The [Middlesex and Boston Street Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middlesex_and_Boston_Street_Railway "Middlesex and Boston Street Railway") came to control the western suburbs, and the [Eastern Massachusetts Street Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Massachusetts_Street_Railway "Eastern Massachusetts Street Railway") came to control the northern and southern suburbs.

Streetcar subways and elevated rail
-----------------------------------

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_the_MBTA&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Streetcar subways and elevated rail")\]

[![Image 6](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4e/Platforms_at_Park_Street_Station%2C_1898.jpg/250px-Platforms_at_Park_Street_Station%2C_1898.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Platforms_at_Park_Street_Station,_1898.jpg)

[Park Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Park_Street_station_/(MBTA/) "Park Street station (MBTA)") on the [Green Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Line_/(MBTA/) "Green Line (MBTA)") soon after opening, circa 1898

Severe streetcar congestion on streets in downtown Boston and the [Great Blizzard of 1888](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Blizzard_of_1888 "Great Blizzard of 1888") created the need for [subways](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rapid_transit "Rapid transit") and elevated rail. These [grade-separated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grade_separation "Grade separation") railways would add transportation capacity, and avoid delays caused by intersections with cross streets and growing congestion in mixed street traffic. The West End Street Railway was renamed the [Boston Elevated Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Elevated_Railway "Boston Elevated Railway") (BERy), and undertook several such projects.

Boston's subway was the first in the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States") and is often called "America's First Subway" by the MBTA and others.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-6) In 1897 and 1898, the [Tremont Street subway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tremont_Street_subway "Tremont Street subway") opened as the core of the precursor to the [Green Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Line_/(MBTA/) "Green Line (MBTA)").[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-7)

In 1901, the [Main Line Elevated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orange_Line_/(MBTA/) "Orange Line (MBTA)"), the precursor to the [Orange Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orange_Line_/(MBTA/) "Orange Line (MBTA)") opened. It was a rapid transit line running as an [elevated railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rapid_transit "Rapid transit") through outlying areas and using the Tremont Street subway downtown, with the outer tracks and platforms reconfigured for Elevated trains.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-Koebel-8) The [Atlantic Avenue Elevated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Avenue_Elevated "Atlantic Avenue Elevated") opened soon after, providing a second route through downtown. This was the first elevated railway and the first rapid transit line in Boston, three years before the first underground line of the [New York City Subway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City_Subway "New York City Subway"), but some 33 years after [the first elevated railway in New York.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IRT_Ninth_Avenue_Line "IRT Ninth Avenue Line")

In 1904, the next line to open was the [East Boston Tunnel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Boston_Tunnel "East Boston Tunnel"), a streetcar tunnel under [Boston Harbor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Harbor "Boston Harbor") to [East Boston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Boston,_Massachusetts "East Boston, Massachusetts"). This replaced a transfer between streetcars and [ferries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferry "Ferry") and provided access to the other subways downtown. The tunnel was converted to [rapid transit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rapid_transit "Rapid transit") specifications in 1924, with an easy cross-platform streetcar transfer at the East Boston end. East Boston ferry continued to run until 1952.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-9)

In 1908, the [Washington Street Tunnel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orange_Line_/(MBTA/) "Orange Line (MBTA)") opened, giving the Elevated a shorter route through downtown and returning the older Tremont Street subway to full streetcar service.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-Koebel-8) Various extensions and branches were built to the Tremont Street subway in both directions, bypassing more surface tracks. In addition, when the Main Line El opened in 1901, many surface routes were cut back to its [Dudley Square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nubian_station "Nubian station") and [Sullivan Square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sullivan_Square_station "Sullivan Square station") terminals to provide a transfer for a faster route downtown. Further elevated extensions, as with the [Charlestown Elevated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlestown_Elevated "Charlestown Elevated"), were soon built on each end, and more streetcar lines were connected.

In 1912, the [Cambridge Tunnel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambridge_Tunnel "Cambridge Tunnel") opened, connecting the Downtown Boston routes to [Harvard Square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_Square "Harvard Square") in [Cambridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambridge,_Massachusetts "Cambridge, Massachusetts"). It was soon extended south from Downtown to [Dorchester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorchester,_Massachusetts "Dorchester, Massachusetts") as the [Dorchester Tunnel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorchester_Tunnel "Dorchester Tunnel"). The Dorchester Extension, opening in stages from 1927, took the line further along a former [New York, New Haven and Hartford Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York,_New_Haven_and_Hartford_Railroad "New York, New Haven and Hartford Railroad") branch through Dorchester, with the [Ashmont–Mattapan High Speed Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mattapan_Line "Mattapan Line") continuing along the old right of way to [Mattapan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mattapan,_Massachusetts "Mattapan, Massachusetts"). This, too, resulted in cutbacks in streetcar service to its terminals.

As built, many of the key rapid transit transfer stations were [prepayment stations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paid_area "Paid area"), in which free transfers could be made between surface streetcar lines and grade-separated subway or elevated lines.
