This was made possible by the operation of all services under one umbrella; some suburban services that operated over the same streetcar tracks used different areas outside [fare control](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paid_area "Paid area"). Some of the streetcar levels in transfer stations were later converted for bus or [trackless trolley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trolleybus "Trolleybus") operation; other such spaces have been closed. Some of the prepaid transfer areas still exist architecturally, and faregates enclose all subway stations (but not most above-ground Green Line stops).

Free in-station transfers were eliminated in October 1961, except among subway routes at the transfer stations in Downtown Boston. Transfers between bus and rapid transit were restored, in a limited capacity in 2000, and in full in 2007 as long as a [CharlieCard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CharlieCard "CharlieCard") is used. Transfers between bus and subway are reduced price but not free, while a single transfer between one local bus and another is free.

Prepayment streetcar stations included rapid transit transfer stations at [Andrew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_station "Andrew station"), [Ashmont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashmont_station "Ashmont station"), [Broadway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broadway_station_/(MBTA/) "Broadway station (MBTA)"), [Dudley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nubian_station "Nubian station"), [Egleston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Egleston_station "Egleston station"), [Everett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everett_station_/(MBTA/) "Everett station (MBTA)"), [Fields Corner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fields_Corner_station "Fields Corner station"), [Forest Hills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forest_Hills_station_/(MBTA/) "Forest Hills station (MBTA)"), [Harvard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_station "Harvard station"), [Lechmere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lechmere_station "Lechmere station"), [Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hynes_Convention_Center_station "Hynes Convention Center station"), [Maverick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maverick_station "Maverick station"), and [Sullivan Square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sullivan_Square_station "Sullivan Square station"); surface-streetcar-only stations at [Arborway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arborway_station "Arborway station"), [Kenmore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenmore_station "Kenmore station"), and [Watertown Yard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Watertown_Yard "Watertown Yard").

### Decline of streetcars and railroads

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_the_MBTA&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Decline of streetcars and railroads")\]

The Boston Elevated Railway started replacing rail vehicles with buses in 1922, a process later dubbed "[bustitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_replacement_bus_service "Rail replacement bus service")". The last Middlesex and Boston Street Railway streetcars ran in 1930. The BERy started replacing some rail vehicles with trackless trolleys in 1936.

By the beginning of 1953, the only [remaining streetcar lines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston-area_streetcar_lines "Boston-area streetcar lines") fed two tunnels — the main [Tremont Street subway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tremont_Street_subway "Tremont Street subway") network downtown and the short tunnel (now the [Harvard bus tunnel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_bus_tunnel "Harvard bus tunnel")) in [Harvard Square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_Square "Harvard Square"). Diesel-powered buses could not be used in the tunnels due to the problem of venting exhaust fumes.

In 1958, the Harvard Square tunnel routes were replaced with electrically powered trackless trolleys, which were the only such MBTA routes. A short non-revenue connection from the terminus of the #71 trackless trolley out of Harvard Square runs to the [Watertown Carhouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Watertown_Yard_/(MBTA_station/) "Watertown Yard (MBTA station)") for maintenance. In the 21st century, with the new Phase 2 [Silver Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silver_Line_/(MBTA/) "Silver Line (MBTA)") in South Boston, trackless trolley services were extended for the first time in decades.

The old elevated railways proved to be an eyesore, and several sharp curves following Boston's twisty streets became more problematic because of severe speed limitations, high maintenance, and noise. The beginning of the decline of the [Atlantic Avenue Elevated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Avenue_Elevated "Atlantic Avenue Elevated") line was the [Boston molasses disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Molasses_Flood "Great Molasses Flood") of 1919, which interrupted service on the line. After another serious accident in 1928, the Atlantic Avenue Elevated was partially closed, running as a stub shuttle. In 1938, it was completely shut down and then demolished for scrap metal in 1942.

In 1944, passenger service on the [Fairmount Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fairmount_Line "Fairmount Line") was canceled by the [New York, New Haven and Hartford Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York,_New_Haven_and_Hartford_Railroad "New York, New Haven and Hartford Railroad") after a long period of declining ridership. As rail passenger service became increasingly unprofitable, largely due to the increasingly popular [automobile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Automobile "Automobile"), government takeover became necessary to prevent abandonment of commuter rail services by bankrupt railroad companies.

### MTA incorporation and takeovers

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_the_MBTA&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: MTA incorporation and takeovers")\]

In 1947, the newly formed Metropolitan Transit Authority (MTA) purchased and took over subway, elevated, streetcar, and bus operations from the [Boston Elevated Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Elevated_Railway "Boston Elevated Railway").[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-10) The original MTA district consisted of 14 cities and towns — [Arlington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arlington,_Massachusetts "Arlington, Massachusetts"), [Belmont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belmont,_Massachusetts "Belmont, Massachusetts"), Boston, [Brookline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookline,_Massachusetts "Brookline, Massachusetts"), [Cambridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambridge,_Massachusetts "Cambridge, Massachusetts"), [Chelsea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chelsea,_Massachusetts "Chelsea, Massachusetts"), [Everett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everett,_Massachusetts "Everett, Massachusetts"), [Malden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malden,_Massachusetts "Malden, Massachusetts"), [Medford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medford,_Massachusetts "Medford, Massachusetts"), [Milton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milton,_Massachusetts "Milton, Massachusetts"), [Newton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newton,_Massachusetts "Newton, Massachusetts"), [Revere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Revere,_Massachusetts "Revere, Massachusetts"), [Somerville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somerville,_Massachusetts "Somerville, Massachusetts"), and [Watertown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Watertown,_Massachusetts "Watertown, Massachusetts").

A state commission headed by Lieutenant Governor [Arthur W. Coolidge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_W._Coolidge "Arthur W. Coolidge") published in 1947 an ambitious plan to replace private commuter rail services (which were losing money) with higher-frequency electric rapid transit that would run roughly out to what is now the [Massachusetts Route 128](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Route_128 "Massachusetts Route 128") corridor. The goal was to shift commuters from automobiles and buses and deal with the "intolerable traffic conditions in downtown Boston".[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-Sweeney-11) The MTA successfully implemented a few rapid transit expansions, but progress was slowed as automobile ownership increased and the [Federal-Aid Highway Act of 1956](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal-Aid_Highway_Act_of_1956 "Federal-Aid Highway Act of 1956") diverted many commuters off of mass transit.

Between 1952 and 1954, the Revere Extension (now part of the [Blue Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Line_/(MBTA/) "Blue Line (MBTA)")) opened to [Wonderland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wonderland_station "Wonderland station"), mostly along the former [narrow-gauge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Narrow-gauge_railway "Narrow-gauge railway") [Boston, Revere Beach and Lynn Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston,_Revere_Beach_and_Lynn_Railroad "Boston, Revere Beach and Lynn Railroad") right-of-way.

In 1959, MTA streetcar service opened on what is now the Riverside [Green Line D branch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Line_D_branch "Green Line D branch"), connecting to the Boylston Street subway and using trackage purchased from the [New York Central Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Central_Railroad "New York Central Railroad"), which had stopped running on the line the previous year. The new service required much more rolling stock than expected, due to heavy ridership.

Also in 1959, with the opening of the [Southeast Expressway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_93 "Interstate 93"), the [New York, New Haven and Hartford Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York,_New_Haven_and_Hartford_Railroad "New York, New Haven and Hartford Railroad") halted passenger service on the former [Old Colony Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Colony_Railroad "Old Colony Railroad") lines. The replacement rapid transit service did not open [until a dozen years later](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Line_/(MBTA/)#South_Shore_line "Red Line (MBTA)"), with the service finally going just beyond [the new Expressway's southern end](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Braintree_Split "Braintree Split") [nine years afterward](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Line_/(MBTA/)#Braintree_extension "Red Line (MBTA)").

Meanwhile, the last two streetcar lines running into the [Pleasant Street Portal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pleasant_Street_Portal "Pleasant Street Portal") of the [Tremont Street subway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tremont_Street_subway "Tremont Street subway") were replaced with buses in 1953 and 1962, and the portal has since been covered over by a public park.

When the MTA reintroduced year-round ferry service to Hull in 1963 (now part of the [MBTA ferry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_ferry "MBTA ferry") system), it was the only commuter-focused ferry service in the United States.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-history-12)

### Formation and commuter rail takeovers

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_the_MBTA&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Formation and commuter rail takeovers")\]

On August 3, 1964, the MBTA succeeded the MTA, with an enlarged service area of 78 cities and towns. A 79th community ([Maynard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maynard,_Massachusetts "Maynard, Massachusetts")) joined in or before 1972 and left in or after 1976.

The MBTA was formed partly to [subsidize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subsidize "Subsidize") existing commuter rail operations, provided at that time by three private railroad companies — the [Boston and Maine Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_and_Maine_Railroad "Boston and Maine Railroad"), the [New York Central Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Central_Railroad "New York Central Railroad") (via the [Boston and Albany Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_and_Albany_Railroad "Boston and Albany Railroad")), and the [New York, New Haven and Hartford Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York,_New_Haven_and_Hartford_Railroad "New York, New Haven and Hartford Railroad") — with the B&M running the north-side lines and the NYC and NYNH&H (both merged into Penn Central in 1968, and taken over by [Conrail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conrail "Conrail") in 1976) on the south side. The MBTA soon began to subsidize the companies, and acquired the lines in stages from 1973 through 1976, but with major cutbacks in service and coverage area. Since then, many of these lines have seen service return, most notably the [Old Colony Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Colony_Railroad "Old Colony Railroad") (NYNH&H) lines to the [South Shore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Shore_/(Boston/) "South Shore (Boston)").

By 1964, commuter rail service to Worcester was being provided. In 1965, the Boston and Maine Railroad started receiving MBTA subsidies for its commuter service. In 1973, the MBTA bought most of its present-day commuter rail trackage from the Boston and Maine Railroad and Penn Central (into which the New York Central Railroad and the New York, New Haven and Hartford Railroad had merged). It also purchased rolling stock at this time. Trackage between Framingham and Worcester was not acquired by the agency, and due to a lack of state subsidy, commuter rail service on this portion was cut in 1975. Service was resumed in 1994, though the track was still privately owned until the state purchased it from CSX Transportation in 2011. The [Fairmount Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fairmount_Line "Fairmount Line") was purchased from Penn Central in 1976. Passenger service resumed there in 1979 during diversion of other lines during [Southwest Corridor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southwest_Corridor_/(Boston/) "Southwest Corridor (Boston)") construction and was continued even after the project was complete.

### Bus expansion and streetcar cutbacks

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_the_MBTA&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Bus expansion and streetcar cutbacks")\]

In 1965, the MBTA assigned colors to its four rapid transit lines on the advice of the [CambridgeSeven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CambridgeSeven "CambridgeSeven") architectural consulting group,[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-Bloomberg-1) and lettered the branches of the Green Line from north to south. However, shortages of streetcars, among other factors, eventually caused bus substitution of rail service on two branches of the Green Line. In 1969, the [A branch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Line_A_branch "Green Line A branch") was replaced by bus service in its entirety. In 1985, the portion of the [E branch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Line_E_branch "Green Line E branch") from [Heath Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heath_Street_/(MBTA_station/) "Heath Street (MBTA station)") to [Arborway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forest_Hills_/(MBTA_station/) "Forest Hills (MBTA station)") was replaced by buses.

In 1968, the MBTA purchased bus routes in the outer suburbs to the north and south, from the [Eastern Massachusetts Street Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Massachusetts_Street_Railway "Eastern Massachusetts Street Railway"). Western suburban routes were purchased in 1972 from the [Middlesex and Boston Street Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middlesex_and_Boston_Street_Railway "Middlesex and Boston Street Railway"). (Both of these companies had long since ceased running any streetcar service). A few routes to the north were taken over from Service Bus Lines in 1975, and one in the south in 1980 from the Brush Hill Transportation Company. As with the commuter rail system, many of the outlying routes were dropped soon before or after the takeover, due to low ridership and high operating costs, and out-of-district communities' refusal to join or contract with the MBTA.

### Rapid transit expansion

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_the_MBTA&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Rapid transit expansion")\]

In the 1970s, the MBTA received a boost from the [BTPR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Transportation_Planning_Review "Boston Transportation Planning Review") areawide re-evaluation of the role of transit relative to highways. Following a moratorium on major highway construction inside Route 128, numerous transit lines were planned for expansion by the Voorhees-Skidmore, Owings and Merrill-ESL consulting team.

The [Charlestown Elevated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlestown_Elevated "Charlestown Elevated"), part of the [Orange Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orange_Line_/(MBTA/) "Orange Line (MBTA)") north of downtown Boston, was replaced by the _Haymarket North Extension_ in 1975.

The _[Braintree extension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Braintree_extension "Braintree extension")_, a branch of the Red Line to [Braintree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Braintree_/(MBTA_station/) "Braintree (MBTA station)"), opened in stages from 1971 to 1980, upgrading an existing rail corridor. The _[Red Line Northwest Extension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Line_Northwest_Extension "Red Line Northwest Extension")_ to [Alewife](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alewife_/(MBTA_station/) "Alewife (MBTA station)") opened in 1985, with an intermediate opening in 1984, partly along a railroad corridor and partly through a newly built deep-bore tunnel.

The southern part of the [Washington Street Elevated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_Street_Elevated "Washington Street Elevated") lasted until 1987 when the [Southwest Corridor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southwest_Corridor_/(Boston/) "Southwest Corridor (Boston)") was opened, rerouting service from discontinued elevated trackage to new facilities in a parallel existing rail corridor. The closure of the Washington Street Elevated south of downtown Boston brought the end of rapid transit service to the [Roxbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roxbury,_Massachusetts "Roxbury, Massachusetts") neighborhood, which was eventually replaced with the [Silver Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silver_Line_/(MBTA/) "Silver Line (MBTA)") [bus rapid transit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bus_rapid_transit "Bus rapid transit").

These extensions provided not only additional subway system coverage but also major [parking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parking "Parking") structures at several of the terminal and intermediate stations. For example, the [Route 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Route_2_/(Massachusetts/) "Route 2 (Massachusetts)") [freeway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freeway "Freeway") ends at the [Red Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Line_/(MBTA/) "Red Line (MBTA)") terminus, [Alewife](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alewife_/(MBTA_station/) "Alewife (MBTA station)") station, where there is a large parking garage operated by the MBTA.

With the 2004 replacement of the [Causeway Street Elevated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Causeway_Street_Elevated "Causeway Street Elevated") by a subway tunnel connection, the only remaining [elevated railways](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rapid_transit "Rapid transit") are a short portion of the [Red Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Line_/(MBTA/) "Red Line (MBTA)") at [Charles/MGH](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles/MGH_/(MBTA_station/) "Charles/MGH (MBTA station)"), and a short portion of the [Green Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Line_/(MBTA/) "Green Line (MBTA)") between [Science Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Science_Park_/(MBTA_station/) "Science Park (MBTA station)") and [Lechmere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lechmere_/(MBTA_station/) "Lechmere (MBTA station)").

### MBTA expansion and the Big Dig

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_the_MBTA&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: MBTA expansion and the Big Dig")\]

In 1999, the district was expanded further to 175 cities and towns, adding most communities that were served by or adjacent to Commuter Rail lines (again including Maynard). The MBTA did not assume responsibility for local transit service in those communities, some of which run their own buses, and some of which depend on private bus services.

Prior to July 1, 2000, the MBTA had been automatically reimbursed by the Commonwealth of Massachusetts for all costs above revenue collected (net cost of service). Beginning on that date, the T was granted a dedicated revenue stream consisting of amounts assessed on served cities and towns, along with a dedicated 20% portion of the 5% state [sales tax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sales_tax "Sales tax"). Going forward, the MBTA now would have to live within this "forward funding" budget.

The Commonwealth assigned to the MBTA responsibility for increasing public transit to compensate for increased automobile pollution from the [Big Dig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Dig "Big Dig"). The T submerged a nearby portion of the Green Line and rebuilt [Haymarket](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haymarket_/(MBTA_station/) "Haymarket (MBTA station)") and [North Stations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Station "North Station") during Big Dig construction. However, these projects have strained the MBTA's limited resources, since the Big Dig project did not include funding for these improvements. Since 1988, the MBTA has been the fastest expanding transit system in the country, even as [Greater Boston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greater_Boston "Greater Boston") has been one of the slowest growing metropolitan areas in the United States.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-wrongtrack-13) When, in 2000, the MBTA's budget became limited, the agency began to run into debt from scheduled projects and obligatory Big Dig remediation work, which have now given the MBTA the highest debt of any transit authority in the country. In an effort to compensate, rates underwent an appreciable hike on January 1, 2007. Increasingly, local advocacy groups are calling on the state to assume $2.9 billion of the authority's now approximate debt of $9 billion, the interest on which severely limits funds available for required projects.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-14)

In 2006, the creation of the [MetroWest Regional Transit Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MetroWest_Regional_Transit_Authority "MetroWest Regional Transit Authority") saw [Framingham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Framingham,_Massachusetts "Framingham, Massachusetts"), [Natick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natick,_Massachusetts "Natick, Massachusetts"), [Weston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weston,_Massachusetts "Weston, Massachusetts"), [Sudbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sudbury,_Massachusetts "Sudbury, Massachusetts"), [Wayland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayland,_Massachusetts "Wayland, Massachusetts"), [Marlborough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marlborough,_Massachusetts "Marlborough, Massachusetts"), [Ashland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashland,_Massachusetts "Ashland, Massachusetts"), [Sherborn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sherborn,_Massachusetts "Sherborn, Massachusetts"), [Hopkinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hopkinton,_Massachusetts "Hopkinton, Massachusetts"), [Holliston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holliston,_Massachusetts "Holliston, Massachusetts"), and [Southborough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southborough,_Massachusetts "Southborough, Massachusetts") subtract their MWRTA assessment from their MBTA assessment. Communities that are also members of other RTAs such as CATA, MVRTA, LRTA, WRTA, [GATRA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greater_Attleboro_Taunton_Regional_Transit_Authority "Greater Attleboro Taunton Regional Transit Authority"), and BAT may also subtract their RTA assessment from their MBTA assessment.\[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\] The amount of funding the MBTA received remained the same; the assessment on remaining cities and towns increased but is still allocated by the same formula.\[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\] On October 31, 2007, the MBTA reestablished [commuter rail service to the Greenbush section](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenbush_Line "Greenbush Line") of [Scituate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scituate,_Massachusetts "Scituate, Massachusetts"), the third branch of the [Old Colony service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Colony_Lines_/(MBTA/) "Old Colony Lines (MBTA)").[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-15) Rail renovation on the [Green Line D branch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Line_D_branch "Green Line D branch") took place in the summer of 2007.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-16) New, low-floor cars on the line were introduced on December 1, 2008.

In 2008, [Daniel Grabauskas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Grabauskas "Daniel Grabauskas"), then the MBTA General Manager, revealed that the MBTA cut trips from published train and bus schedules without informing passengers, referred to as “hidden service cuts”, saying this misrepresentation of service had been happening for years. Grabauskas said this practice has been ended.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-17)

On June 26, 2009, Governor [Deval Patrick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deval_Patrick "Deval Patrick") signed a law to place the MBTA along with other state transportation agencies within the administrative authority of the [Massachusetts Department of Transportation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Department_of_Transportation "Massachusetts Department of Transportation") (MassDOT), with the MBTA now part of the Mass Transit division (MassTrans).[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-Patrick-Press_Release-2009-06-26-18)[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-Transportation_Modernization_Law_2009-19)[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-Boston_Globe-Bierman-2009-01-15-20)[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-Boston_Globe-Bierman-2009-06-18-21) The 2009 transportation law continued the MBTA corporate structure and changed the MBTA board membership to the five Governor-appointed members of the Mass DOT Board.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-Brownsberger-Transport_Reform-2009-06-18-22)

Rhode Island, which has funded commuter rail service to [Providence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Providence_/(Amtrak_station/) "Providence (Amtrak station)") since 1988, paid for extensions of the [Providence/Stoughton Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Providence/Stoughton_Line "Providence/Stoughton Line") to [T.F. Green Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T.F._Green_Airport_/(MBTA_station/) "T.F. Green Airport (MBTA station)") in 2010 and [Wickford Junction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wickford_Junction_/(MBTA_station/) "Wickford Junction (MBTA station)") in 2012. The [Fairmount Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fairmount_Line "Fairmount Line"), located entirely in the southern reaches of Boston, has been undergoing an improvement project since 2002. The first new station, [Talbot Avenue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_Avenue_station "Talbot Avenue station"), opened in November 2012.[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-globetalbot-23)

### Debt concerns, route cutbacks, and fare increases

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_the_MBTA&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Debt concerns, route cutbacks, and fare increases")\]

Claims have been made by the Pioneer Institute that since 1988 the MBTA has been the fastest expanding transit system in the country, even as [Greater Boston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greater_Boston "Greater Boston") has been the slowest growing metropolitan area.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-wrongtrack-13) However, research by the Frontier Group finds that "no category has the MBTA been the “fastest-growing” of the nation's largest transit agencies, and in only two categories does it crack the top 10. However, the MBTA does crack the top 10 in another category: absolute growth in transit ridership."[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-24)

When, in 2000, the MBTA's income was capped, the agency began to run up large debts from already-scheduled projects and obligatory Big Dig remediation work. As of 2012, the MBTA has the highest debt of any transit authority in the United States. In an effort to compensate, rates were hiked on January 1, 2007, from $1.25 up to $2.00 per subway ride with a [CharlieTicket](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CharlieCard "CharlieCard"), and $1.70 with a CharlieCard.[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-25) Increasingly, local advocacy groups are calling on the state to assume $2.9 billion of the authority's debt, which totals approximately $9 billion. The interest on this debt is a large proportion of the MBTA's annual expenses, and severely limits funds available for any further required projects.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-26)

In April 2012, the MBTA Advisory Board approved major fare increases on all MBTA services, and cutbacks or terminations of some transit routes. In July 2014, fares were increased further by an average of 5%.

On October 10, 2007, the MBTA introduced a pilot program in North, South, and Airport stations called T-Radio. The program would have been expanded to pipe in music, light news, weather, entertainment tips, and eight to ten minutes of commercials each hour to every MBTA subway station.[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-27) After the agency received an overwhelming number of e-mails — 1,800, mostly complaints — it decided to shelve the program on October 25.[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-28)

On May 28, 2008, a westbound trolley on the [Green Line D branch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Line_D_branch "Green Line D branch") slammed into a stopped train between the [Waban](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waban_/(MBTA_station/) "Waban (MBTA station)") and [Woodland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woodland_/(MBTA_station/) "Woodland (MBTA station)") stations shortly after 6 p.m. At least seven people were injured, and the operator of the moving train, Terrese Edmonds, 24, was killed.[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-29) On May 8, 2009, two Green Line trolleys collided between [Park Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Park_Street_station_/(MBTA/) "Park Street station (MBTA)") and [Government Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_Center_/(MBTA_station/) "Government Center (MBTA station)") when the driver of one of them, 24-year-old Aiden Quinn, was [text messaging](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Text_messaging "Text messaging") his girlfriend.[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-30) A rule banning cell phones for operators while driving their bus, train, or streetcar was put into place days later.[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-31)

Immediately following the [Boston Marathon bombing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Marathon_bombing "Boston Marathon bombing"), the MBTA was partially shut down and National Guardsmen were deployed in various stations around the city.[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-32) During the ensuing manhunt for Dzhokhar and Tamerlan Tsarnaev the MBTA was fully shut down until the stay-inside request for Watertown, Newton, Waltham, Cambridge, Belmont, and Boston was lifted.[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-33) During the manhunt, MBTA buses were used to ferry police around the city. After the suspect was caught the MBTA resumed normal service. The next day the MBTA began displaying "BOSTON STRONG" and "WE ARE ONE BOSTON" on buses and subway cars, in addition to the destination that is normally displayed.[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-34)

### Charlie Baker administration (2015–2023)

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_the_MBTA&action=edit&section=21 "Edit section: Charlie Baker administration (2015–2023)")\]

#### Crisis and appointment of control board

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_the_MBTA&action=edit&section=22 "Edit section: Crisis and appointment of control board")\]

In February 2015, there was [record breaking snowfall in Boston from the 2014–15 North American winter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014%E2%80%9315_North_American_winter#Northeastern_United_States "2014–15 North American winter") causing a partial shutdown and severe delays on all [MBTA subway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_subway "MBTA subway") lines,[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-35) and many long-term operational and financial problems with the entire MBTA system came under greater public attention.[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-36)[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-37) [Massachusetts Governor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor_of_Massachusetts "Governor of Massachusetts") [Charlie Baker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlie_Baker "Charlie Baker") indicated at the time that he was reluctant to discuss the financing issues but that he would "have more to say about that in a couple of weeks."[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-38)

Following criticism of his emergency management and polling demonstrating public opinion in favor of his administration prioritizing resolving the MBTA's issues,[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-39)[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-40) Baker announced the formation of a special advisory panel to diagnose the MBTA's problems and write a report recommending proposals to address them.[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-41) The special advisory panel released its report that April.[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-42) The report was broadly critical of MBTA operational and financial management, noting that the system was in "severe financial distress", was "governed ineffectively", spent inefficiently, and had a high-absentee workplace culture.[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-43) Among other reforms, the report recommended suspending the governance of the agency by the [MassDOT Board of Directors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Department_of_Transportation#Mass_Transit_Division "Massachusetts Department of Transportation"); replacing it with a temporary Fiscal and Management Control Board directly appointed by the Governor and the leadership of the state legislature; expanding the existing MassDOT Board; and adding term limits.[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-44) The MassDOT Board resigned on Baker's request the following week.[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-45) Legislation, which closely followed the report's recommendations,[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-46) passed the following July[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-47) along with the appointment of the Fiscal and Management Control Board.[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-48)[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-49) Baker also appointed a new MassDOT Board of Directors and proposed a five-year, $83 million winter resiliency plan.[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-50)[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-51)

After initially blaming the snowfall and a lack of public investment in an aging system for the crisis,[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-52) MBTA General Manager Beverly Scott announced her resignation effective April 11.[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-53) MassDOT Chief Operating Officer and Highway Division Administrator Frank DePaola was appointed to fill Scott's position.[\[54\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-54) DePaola retired June 30, 2016, and was replaced with Brian Shortsleeve.[\[55\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-55) Shortsleeve swapped positions with Fiscal and Management Control Board vice chair Steve Poftak on June 30, 2017.[\[56\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-:0-56) Baker launched a search for a permanent MBTA General Manager in February 2017.[\[57\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-57)

That August, the MBTA named former [General Electric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Electric "General Electric") executive Luis Ramirez to be its new general manager.[\[58\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-58) Ramirez's previous management experience, as well as the process for vetting him,[\[59\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-59) came under public scrutiny and criticism because of a twice-dismissed [class action](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Class_action "Class action") lawsuit during his tenure as CEO of the [Dallas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dallas "Dallas")\-based Global Power Equipment Group.[\[60\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-60)[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-61) Even so, Baker spoke in favor of Ramirez,[\[62\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-62) who began his tenure as MBTA General Manager on September 12, 2017.[\[63\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-63) Ramirez left the position effective January 1, 2019, and was replaced by Steve Poftak.[\[64\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-64) In June 2021, the Fiscal and Management Control Board was dissolved,[\[65\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-65) and the following month, Baker signed into law a supplemental budget bill that included a provision creating a permanent MBTA Board of Directors and Baker appointed the new board the following October.[\[66\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-66)[\[67\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-67)

Injuries involving a Green Line collision and Back Bay escalator malfunction, a dragging death on the Red Line, a fatal Commuter Rail collision with a car, and a death resulting from a fall through a rusty staircase attracted considerable public attention.[\[68\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-68) In April 2022, the [Federal Transit Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Transit_Administration "Federal Transit Administration") announced in a letter to general manager Poftak that it would assume an increased safety oversight role over the MBTA and would conduct a safety management inspection.[\[69\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-69)[\[70\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-70)

The FTA soon found subway dispatchers working 20-hour shifts due to a staffing shortage. The MBTA cut rush hour service frequency on the Red, Blue, and Orange Lines to allow dispatchers and subway supervisors adequate rest.[\[71\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-71) Federal inspectors also issued emergency directives concerning runaway trains in yards, and the backlog of track maintenance, which caused about 10% of the subway system to be under speed restriction.[\[72\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-72) After an Orange Line train fire endangered hundreds of passengers and caused one to jump off a bridge into the [Mystic River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mystic_River "Mystic River"), the MBTA decided to shut down the entire Orange Line for 30 days to accelerate track work and re-open with all new subway cars.[\[73\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-73) In December 2022, the Orange Line was unable to meet even its reduced schedule when about half the trains were pulled from service without notice to passengers, due to problems with electrical arcing.[\[74\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-74)

The full FTA safety report released in August 2022[\[75\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-75) demanded an increase in staffing and retention of senior employees; collection of, prioritization of, and decision-making based on safety-related risks, failures, and precursors; clarification of safety communication-related procedures for frontline workers; oversight of failures to implement safety requirements; more resources for formal technical training; addressing radio dead zones; more independent quality assurance; more active and independent safety oversight by the [Massachusetts Department of Public Utilities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Department_of_Public_Utilities "Massachusetts Department of Public Utilities").[\[76\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-76)

#### Service cuts and improvements

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_the_MBTA&action=edit&section=24 "Edit section: Service cuts and improvements")\]

In June 2015, the MBTA scaled back the schedule for a one-year pilot program to expand late-night service on weekends,[\[77\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-77) having expanded it that February.[\[78\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-78) The program was cut in March 2016.[\[79\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-79) Despite this setback, improvements were made to service during this time. In October 2015, the MBTA announced that the [Commuter Rail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_Commuter_Rail "MBTA Commuter Rail") was adding nonstop trips during peak commute times along the [Framingham/Worcester Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Framingham/Worcester_Line "Framingham/Worcester Line") between [Back Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Back_Bay_station "Back Bay station") and [Worcester Union Stations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_Station_/(Worcester,_Massachusetts/) "Union Station (Worcester, Massachusetts)").[\[80\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-80) In March 2016, the MBTA reopened [Government Center Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_Center_station_/(MBTA/) "Government Center station (MBTA)") after two years of construction upgrades.[\[81\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-81) In September 2016, a month after Baker signed into law a regulatory framework for [ridesharing companies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ridesharing_company "Ridesharing company"),[\[82\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-82) Baker and the MBTA announced a pilot program partnering the MBTA's [The Ride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ride_/(MBTA/) "The Ride (MBTA)") with [Uber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uber "Uber") and [Lyft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyft "Lyft") to improve [paratransit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paratransit "Paratransit") services for [disabled](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disability "Disability") riders,[\[83\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-83) which was expanded the following February to all users of The Ride.[\[84\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-84)

In December 2016, the MBTA Fiscal and Management Control Board approved a proposal to replace all [MBTA Red Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Line_/(MBTA/) "Red Line (MBTA)") fleet vehicles by 2025.[\[85\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-85) In January 2017, the MBTA announced that the new [Boston Landing Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Landing_station "Boston Landing station") on the [Commuter Rail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_Commuter_Rail "MBTA Commuter Rail")'s [Framingham/Worcester Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Framingham/Worcester_Line "Framingham/Worcester Line") would open the following May.[\[86\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-86) A groundbreaking for the $38.5 million renovation of [Ruggles Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruggles_station "Ruggles station"), in [Roxbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roxbury,_Boston "Roxbury, Boston"), occurred that August.[\[87\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-87) In April 2017, the [Federal Transit Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Transit_Administration "Federal Transit Administration") approved a revised cost estimate for the [Green Line Extension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Line_Extension "Green Line Extension") proposed by the MBTA Fiscal and Management Control Board and the MassDOT Board of Directors, allowing the project to be eligible for federal funding.[\[88\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-88)[\[89\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-89) The Green Line Extension broke ground in [Somerville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somerville,_Massachusetts "Somerville, Massachusetts") in June of the following year.[\[90\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-90)

In April 2018, the MBTA began a one-year pilot program for early morning bus service along certain [MBTA bus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_bus "MBTA bus") routes in [Boston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston "Boston") (which the Fiscal and Management Control Board voted to make permanent the following December),[\[91\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-91)[\[92\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-92) and the [MBTA Silver Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silver_Line_/(MBTA/) "Silver Line (MBTA)") began operating a route from [Chelsea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chelsea_station_/(MBTA/) "Chelsea station (MBTA)") to [South Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Station "South Station").[\[93\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-93) In June 2018, the MBTA began a 3-month pilot of a summer weekend [Commuter Rail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_Commuter_Rail "MBTA Commuter Rail") fare of $10 for unlimited use, which was subsequently extended another three months.[\[94\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-94)[\[95\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-95) Also in June 2018, the MBTA announced parking fee changes based on parking lot usage,[\[96\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-96) and the MBTA released estimates showing that the proposed [North–South Rail Link](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North%E2%80%93South_Rail_Link "North–South Rail Link") would cost between $12.3 billion and $21.5 billion.[\[97\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-97) In January 2019, following a one-month hiatus, MBTA General Manager Steve Poftak announced that the [Federal Transit Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Transit_Administration "Federal Transit Administration") approved a six-month extension of the Commuter Rail weekend fare pilot beginning that month,[\[98\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-98) which the Fiscal and Management Control Board voted to make permanent the following March.[\[99\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-99)

#### Budget balancing and fares

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_the_MBTA&action=edit&section=25 "Edit section: Budget balancing and fares")\]

In August 2015, MBTA officials released revised estimates of the MBTA's State-of-Good-Repair backlog upwards to $7.3 billion.[\[100\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-100) While MBTA officials announced the following month that advertising revenue was running 26 percent higher that year than at the same time the previous year,[\[101\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-101) the Fiscal and Management Control Board released its first report. The board report showed that the MBTA's operating expenses and debt service were growing nearly three times the rate of revenue growth—being projected to grow from a projected $170 million in fiscal year 2016 to a projected $427 million by fiscal year 2020 if left unaddressed—and that operator absences accounted for 69 percent of the 34,347 dropped bus runs and subway trips between January and August of that year.[\[102\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-WBUR_9-22-2015-102)[\[103\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-103) The Fiscal and Management Control Board voted to increase fares across the system by an average of 9.3 percent that March.[\[104\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-104) However, according to an April 2016 estimate, the agency was losing $42 million per year due to [fare evasion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fare_evasion "Fare evasion") (amounting to approximately one-fourth of the agency's $170 million operating budget deficit in fiscal year 2016).[\[105\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-105)[\[102\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-WBUR_9-22-2015-102) In June 2016, the MBTA Fiscal and Management Control Board voted unanimously to indefinitely extend a pilot program of discounted passes for low-income youths and to increase the maximum age for participation in the program to 25.[\[106\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-106)

In July 2016, after the Fiscal and Management Control Board completed its first year, Baker addressed the status of MBTA operations and financial management. There was significant progress, including a leveling of the MBTA operating expense budget between the 2015 and 2016 fiscal years (after a 5 percent per year increase over the previous 15 years), a 25 percent decline in operator absenteeism, a 30 percent decline in overtime expenses, a one-third decline in dropped bus runs, and improvements to system infrastructure.[\[107\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-107) However, at the same time, Baker noted that the MBTA was "still in very tough shape", reiterating concerns about the MBTA pension system,[\[108\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-108) the security of the MBTA's cash-handling operations,[\[109\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-109) need for reform to the MBTA's procurement and contracting system, and improvements to its infrastructure maintenance system highlighted in the advisory panel report.[\[110\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-110) Also in July 2016, Baker signed into law a bill capping MBTA fare increases to 7 percent once every two years.[\[111\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-111)

In October 2016, the MBTA Fiscal and Management Control Board voted to outsource the MBTA's cash-handling operations to the security company [Brink's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brink%27s "Brink's") on a $18.7 million, five-year contract, a decision opposed by unions and elected officials.[\[112\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-WBUR_10-6-2016-112)[\[113\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-Metzger_10-12-2016-113) The MBTA also extended its existing contract with the Boston Carmen's Union in December 2016 through 2021 with new wage structures that would reduce the MBTA's operating budget by $80 million over the subsequent four years.[\[114\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-114) The following month, the agency outsourced its warehousing and parts-delivery operations to an external vendor for $28.4 million on a five-year contract.[\[115\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-115)

In April 2017, the Fiscal and Management Control Board approved a $1.98 billion budget which reduced the MBTA operating budget deficit from $42 million to $30 million.[\[116\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-116) The following month, Baker approved the Fiscal and Management Control Board's request to exercise the two-year extension option to continue its governance of the MBTA allowed under the law that authorized its formation.[\[56\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-:0-56) In July 2017, interim MBTA General Manager Steve Poftak said that the MBTA would accelerate its capital spending from an average of $437 million (excluding expansion projects) in the previous five years to $702 million for fiscal year 2019.[\[117\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-117) Simultaneously, Poftak also noted that the MBTA was "saving money" by outsourcing "ancillary" operations to vendors.[\[118\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-118)

In November 2017, the MBTA Fiscal and Management Control Board voted to award a 13-year contract for $723 million to the [Cubic Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cubic_Corporation "Cubic Corporation") to design, implement, and operate a new fare collection system for the MBTA by 2020.[\[119\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-119) In February 2018, MBTA General Manager Luis Ramirez announced to the Fiscal and Management Control Board that the MBTA would face a $111 million operating budget deficit for fiscal year 2019.[\[120\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-120) However, that August, MBTA officials announced that the agency had finished the 2018 fiscal year with a balanced operating budget for the first time in a decade.[\[121\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-121)

In February 2020, the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic") began to impact Massachusetts. When the stay-at-home advisory was issued the following month, businesses closed or sent staff to work from home, and people were advised to avoid riding public transit unless necessary. At the lowest point, MBTA ridership dropped about 78% on buses, 92% on the subway, on 71% paratransit, and 97% on commuter rail.[\[122\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-122) Bus and subway ran on a modified Saturday schedule; commuter rail was on a reduced schedule and ferries were shut down completely. To facilitate social distancing from drivers, buses started running fare-free with rear-door-only boarding, passengers were required to wear face masks (except small children and people with relevant medical conditions), and the agency began frequently sanitizing vehicles and stations. Driver availability was limited as some employees contracted the virus. The T received $827 million in federal aid for FY2020 and FY2021 to make up for increased costs and lost revenue.[\[123\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-123)

In June, the MBTA announced that commuter rail tickets and passes valid as of March 10 would be valid for 90 days, starting on June 22. It also made various fare changes to encourage riders to shift from potentially crowded bus or subway, including discounted ten-ride tickets, half-price tickets for youth, and Zone 1A fares extended to Lynn and River Works stations.[\[124\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-124)

#### 2021 budget proposal

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_the_MBTA&action=edit&section=27 "Edit section: 2021 budget proposal")\]

Due to the COVID-19 pandemic, [ridership](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patronage_/(transportation/) "Patronage (transportation)") on the MBTA has declined by 87%[\[125\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-:5-125) which has forced Massachusetts legislators and the MBTA to potentially implement a plan that would eliminate weekend commuter rail services and shut it down after 9 p.m. on weeknights, eliminate 25 bus routes, stop subway and bus services at midnight, among other changes to scale back services. This plan, if implemented through a vote by the Fiscal and Management Control Board, would save Massachusetts more than $130 million. The loss in services could potentially mean that up to 1,700 riders will not be able to take the bus and 733 riders will not be able to take the train. Supporters of this plan believe that this is the best plan as the majority of ridership has decreased due to the pandemic and it is not feasible to continue providing services that would not be used, especially if there are alternatives to using [public transportation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_transport "Public transport"), such as personal vehicles. Through saving money by cutting services, the city is planning on using the money for services once the pandemic has ended.[\[126\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-:4-126) Supporters claim that reduced services will still be sufficient for those who still rely on public transport during the pandemic. Changes would not be implemented right away, rather, they could slowly be introduced, with the earliest changes coming in January 2021 and other changes coming as late as summer 2021. This allows the MBTA to adjust service needs based on ridership needs.[\[127\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-127) On the other hand, opponents argue that by reducing services, it will be harder for riders, who are typically low-income or people of color to get to essential jobs. Riders will be forced to find other ways of transportation, which could mean using [personal vehicles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vehicle "Vehicle"), leading to an increase in dependence on the [automobility paradigm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paradigm "Paradigm").[\[126\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-:4-126) Opponents argue that public transportation should be treated as a public good, which means asking wealthier people and corporations to pay their share for the upkeep of transportation as a way to achieve [mobility justice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Justice "Justice").[\[125\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_MBTA#cite_note-:5-125)

15.content:
The MBTA’s approach to energy management consists of three fundamental ideas:

1.  Reduce the use of fossil fuels 
2.  Invest in renewable and clean energy 
3.  Efficient management of energy assets

By taking a holistic approach to energy management, we can reduce our carbon footprint, use energy more efficiently, and stabilize our energy budget.

As of January 2021, the MBTA is powered by 100% renewable electricity.

**Renewable Energy Resources**
------------------------------

The MBTA will purchase its electricity and Renewable Energy Credits (RECs) from renewable energy providers in New England.

Benefits include:

*   The MBTA can certify the use of renewable energy in its portfolio
*   RECs provide a dedicated stake in electricity produced from certified renewable energy power plants
*   RECs allow energy producers to finance new clean energy projects in the region

In addition to the purchase of renewable energy, the MBTA has some on-site renewable energy infrastructure in various locations on MBTA property, with more to come. The projects below are just a few that will help the MBTA meet our clean energy goal.

### Wind Energy

![Image 1: Close up view of the MBTA's wind turbine in Kingston Massachusetts. ](https://cdn.mbta.com/sites/default/files/styles/max_2600x2600/public/media/2020-10/wind-turbine-closeup.JPG?itok=r-glMLMz)

The are two MBTA wind turbines:

#### **The Kingston Turbine**

Located near the Kingston Commuter Rail station, it powers both the station and the adjacent layover facility. Energy created by this turbine is:

*   Used to power station lighting
*   Used to power the units that keep train engines warm overnight in cold weather (without this clean energy, trains would need to idle overnight to keep from freezing)

#### **The Bridgewater Turbine**

Located near the Bridgewater Commuter Rail station, it powers both the station and the adjacent layover facility. Energy created by this turbine:

*   Is returned back to the local electrical grid for use by others
*   Acts as an offset for electricity consumed by the MBTA at other locations

Funding for both turbines is provided by:

*   The Federal Transit Administration (FTA) 
*   The Transportation Investments for Greenhouse Gas and Energy Reductions (TIGGER) 
*   A grant from the Massachusetts Clean Energy Center (MassCEC)

[View the FMCB presentation on Electricity Procurement](https://cdn.mbta.com/sites/default/files/2020-10/2020-10-05-fmcb-M-electricity-procurement-accessible.pdf)

### Solar Energy

![Image 2: mbta solar canopy at nantasket station parking lot](https://cdn.mbta.com/sites/default/files/styles/max_2600x2600/public/media/2020-12/nantasket-solar-canopy.JPG?itok=TpDwPnXf)

The MBTA partnered with Altus Power to install, operate, and maintain solar canopies at MBTA parking lots.

As of 2022, there are five solar canopies generating energy on MBTA property, with the potential to create more than three megawatts of solar energy capacity. These canopies expand the Commonwealth’s renewable energy portfolio and reduce the cost of electricity and snow removal for the MBTA.

We've also installed small-scale solar energy arrays at [Orient Heights station](https://www.mbta.com/stops/place-orhte), and we plan to add more solar panels with new capital projects. The MBTA remains committed to evaluating and pursuing new opportunities to add renewable energy generation across its properties.

Building a Better T
-------------------

As part of our $9.6 billion, [5-year capital investment plan](https://www.mbta.com/cip), we're renovating stations, modernizing fare collection systems, upgrading services for our buses, subways, and ferries, and improving the accessibility of the entire system.

[Learn more](https://www.mbta.com/projects)

Energy Efficiency Upgrades
--------------------------

![Image 3: A crewman installs new lights above the Green Line at Park Street](https://cdn.mbta.com/sites/default/files/styles/max_2600x2600/public/media/2020-01/GL_ParkStreet_Lighting-2020-01-19-5911.jpg?itok=vLa8woy2)

More than 70,000 light fixtures help MBTA customers navigate through stations and platforms.

Until recently, the majority of these fixtures used inefficient fluorescent bulbs. Swapping those out for T-8 and induction fixtures has saved the MBTA $783 for every kW, or nearly $1 million a year.

Over the past few years, the MBTA has implemented over 90 energy efficiency projects that have resulted in an energy reduction of 75 million kWH and 117 million pounds of greenhouse gases.

Projects include upgrades to:

*   Station and facility lighting
*   Boilers and HVAC systems
*   Equipment (pumps, motors, drives, compressed air, etc.)

The MBTA has partnered with two local utility companies (National Grid and Eversource) for a Three-Year (FY21–FY23) Energy Efficiency Program. This program includes $28 million in capital investments for energy upgrades at 85 MBTA facilities.

Upon completion of these, the MBTA will save over 30 million kWh of electricity and 47 million tons of greenhouse gases. This will also result in significant financial savings.

Recently, we upgraded the track and switch heater systems, which dramatically reduced energy usage.

Work included adding 700 energy-efficient heaters for the track system. With this upgrade, the heater system is now centrally controlled in the MBTA Control Center so we can control when the heaters are turned on—previously, heaters were turned on in November and turned off in April. As of 2020, we are able to turn the heaters on manually—and only when the weather drops below 38 degrees.

This saves 31 million kWH of electricity and 48.3 million pounds of greenhouse gases. To further improve this system, we will tie the heating system to a cloud-based weather station so that the units are turned on and off automatically.

MBTA signals are lit by 2,300 specially-made LED bulbs. While the old incandescent signal bulbs lasted only six weeks, the new LED bulbs can last up to eight years, using a fraction of the energy of an incandescent.

In the first three years after the bulbs were installed, the MBTA was able to save over $1 million in maintenance costs for signal lights.

Tracking Energy Consumption
---------------------------

To track and manage energy consumption, the MBTA uses an Enterprise Energy Management System (EEMS) to closely monitor energy consumption and billings to see if there are aberrations or areas where energy consumption is too high. This system provides critical data for the  more than 600 utility accounts in the MBTA system.

Among other metrics, the EEMS tracks “Energy Consumption per Passenger Trip” and “Energy Consumption per Mile.” The current system includes data from 2009 to today and tracks the use of electricity, diesel, gasoline, compressed natural gas (CNG), steam, and jet fuel.

[### Sustainability and Resilience at the MBTA](https://www.mbta.com/sustainability)![Image 4: Aerial view of the T's solar canopy covering a parking lot in West Hingham.](https://live-mbta.pantheonsite.io/sites/default/files/styles/teaser/public/media/2020-10/west-hingham-solar-canopy.JPG?itok=Zj_Mv6v5)

The MBTA plays an important role in reducing emissions in Massachusetts. Our goal is to increase sustainability and enhance the resilience of the transit system, further strengthening the climate benefits of our public transportation services.

5.content:
When the Plymouth Independent site went live on Nov. 21 of last year, the first batch of stories included one by Fred Thys about the status of the MBTA commuter rail station at Cordage Park. The headline read: “You still can’t get there from here.”

More than a year later – and three and a half years after the tracks were deserted – nothing has changed. You still can’t travel to and from Plymouth by train. The April 2021 closure was blamed on budget cuts at the then-reeling T, and a dramatic drop in ridership because of the pandemic. The agency framed the shutdown as “temporary.” Few believed that then. Almost no one does now. It’s kind of like exercising – once you stop doing it, starting up again is a challenge.

Not a week goes by that I don’t get asked whether rail service will come back to Plymouth. Often, the questions come from people who are relatively new to town. To them, it’s puzzling that the region’s population hub does not have a direct link to Boston. On the face of it, they’re correct. With the town growing at a steady pace, you might think transportation officials would figure the demand for commuter rail from Plymouth is strong and will increase.

Think again.

From the vantage point of MBTA and state officials, the local stop has long been irrelevant. There is a much bigger station, with plenty of parking, just over the border in Kingston. Plymouth ridership numbers were always slim, partly because trips were few and far between. And while the Kingston station is easily accessible from Route 3, Plymouth’s forlorn platform is off a secondary road (Route 3A), hidden behind the Harborwalk apartment complex. If you’re coming from outside the town’s center, it’s easier to go to Kingston.

Never mind that for hundreds of people who live at Harborwalk, the promised proximity to commuter rail was a key selling point – walk out the door and onto a train. Beats the expressway by about 40 miles and hours of stress, right?

When I asked the T for an update on the station’s status, I wasn’t expecting any revelations. I was correct.

“The MBTA is committed to exploring service opportunities that best serve the riding public as a whole,” spokesperson Lisa Battiston wrote in an email. “At this time, Plymouth station remains closed due to operational challenges associated with serving the station. Passengers can use Kingston station for service to and from downtown Boston.”

After the trains stopped in 2021, the T coordinated with the Greater Attleboro and Taunton Regional Transit Authority, known as GATRA, to make sure there were frequent bus trips from Plymouth to Kingston for travelers who can’t – or don’t want to – drive to the station.

But that’s not enough for some Plymouth business leaders and elected officials.

Amy Naples, executive director of the Plymouth Area Chamber of Commerce, which has more than 800 members, wrote me to “express deep concern over the MBTA’s continued closure of the Plymouth station.” She called it “profoundly disheartening to see the existing infrastructure – tracks, platforms, and facilities – sitting idle, offering no benefit to the community or region. This dormant resource represents a missed opportunity for connectivity and growth, as the station remains a vital link for residents, visitors, and businesses alike.”

Beyond that, Naples said, the continued closure “threatens to derail critical economic development projects and continued growth at Cordage Commerce Center and Harborwalk Apartments, which rely on public transit to attract residents and businesses. Losing this service harms local tourism and small businesses, diminishing Plymouth’s appeal as a destination for visitors from Boston and beyond.”

![Image 1](https://www.plymouthindependent.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/IMG_6248-rotated.jpg)

The tilting sign may say “temporarily closed,” but it’s been there since April 2021. Credit: (Photo by Mark Pothier)

Incoming state senator Dylan Fernandes, who calls himself a “huge fan of train transportation,” says the station closure came up regularly on the campaign trail. With train travel, he said in an interview, “you actually get somewhere and get work done at the same time. It takes cars off the roads, reduces carbon emissions, and is overall a benefit for society.”

Once sworn into office, Fernandes said, he plans to “open up a dialogue” with the T and the Healy administration. It bothers him that the state appears to be “sitting on unused infrastructure that is upgraded and good to go if they re-open it.”

He’s also pragmatic. Restarting service to Plymouth is “obviously not something you can single handedly do,” Fernandes said, “but you can advocate for it.”

Matt Muratore, the outgoing state representative, agrees with Fernandes about the need for train trips to and from Plymouth. He also knows how tough it will be to make that happen.

“The meetings we’ve had in the last year or so \[on the subject\] haven’t been so promising,” Muratore told me. “As you know, the MBTA is having its own issues in and around the Boston area, and the concentration is really there, not so much down here.”

When Covid hit, “We said ‘please don’t shut it down.’ Because we knew that once it was shut down, it’s a hard thing to get back up and running again. The rest is history.”

Muratore said the Plymouth stop was never given much of a chance to succeed.

“The schedule wasn’t that great,” he said. “I think it was two or three times a day.”

Not exactly commuter friendly.

By contrast, there are typically a dozen or trips to and from Kingston on weekdays, between 5:30 a.m. and 11:15 p.m.

“They don’t really want to open it,” Muratore conceded, “but we’re still trying to advocate to do that. I still think it’s the right thing to do.”

But there’s a twist in this story that you probably didn’t see coming. An argument can be made for letting the station remain idle, and it has nothing to do with Plymouth’s transportation needs. Under the state’s controversial MBTA Communities Act – passed in 2021 just months before the Cordage stop went dark – the town would lose its status as an MBTA “adjacent” community, meaning it would have to create a zoning overlay that would allow more, denser housing within about a half mile of Cordage than is now required. The idea behind the law is to encourage cities and towns with rail service to build more homes close to public transportation. The concept is complicated, as all things having to do with Beacon Hill are. It doesn’t work so well in Plymouth because of the town’s geographic size – about 105 square miles – and the fact that the area around Cordage already is densely populated.

The numbers sound scary. Under the current status, the town must allow for 2,807 housing units, but they don’t have to be built near commuter rail, according to Lee Hartmann, Plymouth’s director of planning and development.

If the station reopens, however, that figure would increase to 4,210. Crucially, the additional housing would have to be located within a half mile of Cordage. That’s because Plymouth would lose its “adjacent” designation and be subject to more stringent requirements. While the law does not demand that all those homes be built, it makes it easier for developers to go ahead with projects.

“If such zoning was put in place, it would over time significantly change the character of North Plymouth,” Hartmann said.

Does that mean that the station’s shutdown allowed the town to avoid a housing crisis of sorts (even though it needs more housing in the long run)? Select Board member Kevin Canty believes that’s the case. Plymouth’s existing status allows for more “flexibility,” he said.

“The total number of \[housing\] units is smaller, and they can be spread out through the entire 105 square miles,” Canty said in a phone conversation.

(In case you were wondering, the Harborwalk complex by itself doesn’t come close to fulfilling the housing requirement.)

There is hope that the law could be modified. The Communities Act has faced resistance from officials and voters in some of the 177 cities and towns covered by it. The rebellion started with Milton, which is being sued by the state for non-compliance after voters rejected its terms in February. The case has gone to the Supreme Judicial Court. As it stands now, though, a community that refuses to comply with the act risks losing state funding for such needs as road, bridge, water, and sewer work.

“We believe that there is some likelihood that the law will change in some way due to pushback from some of the other communities,” Canty said. “We didn’t want Plymouth to fundamentally change its character and makeup to comply with a law now that may change in two or three years to be more favorable.”

Regardless, Canty doubts there is enough demand to make direct rail service between Plymouth and Boston viable. At least not out of Cordage.

“The last few years it was in operation, it was barely doing anything,” he said. “You would’ve been hard pressed to reliably use that to get in and out of Boston. That’s why when I used to take the commuter rail into Boston years ago, I would go to Kingston. A lot of Plymouth residents, even if this station came back online, would find themselves doing the same thing…People say, if we send the trains they will come. I don’t think that’s going to happen.”

_Mark Pothier can be reached at [mark@plymouthindependent.org](mailto:mark@plymouthindependent.org). One other thing: Unlike our news stories, this column includes the author’s opinions._

**Translate:  [to English](https://www-wind--watch-org.translate.goog/newsarchive/2011/08/12/mbta-plans-wind-turbine-at-commuter-rail-facility/print/?_x_tr_sl=auto&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en-US) | to other**

**Translate:  _FROM_ English | _TO_ English**

The MBTA has chosen a contractor to erect a 120-foot-high, 100-kilowatt wind turbine near the commuter rail station in Kingston, officials said.

SPS New England submitted the lowest bid at $334,334.50, the MBTA said today in a statement. The project will be located at the layover facility near the station, a set of tracks where trains are parked overnight.

When the project is completed at the end of the year, the turbine is expected to generate enough energy to cover 65 percent of the Kingston station’s power needs, such as the parking lot and platform lighting, and electric power for parked locomotives with engines switched off.

Construction will begin next month.

A second wind turbine is expected to be built next year at the Bridgewater commuter rail station. Estimates say that the turbines will save the MBTA about $100,000 in electricity costs annually, MBTA General Manager Richard Davey said.

“As part of our efforts to implement green efforts here at MBTA, we’ve sought ways to improve our renewable energy portfolio. And one way we’ve done that is win federal grants to have wind turbines installed on our property,” Davey said.
