You still can’t get there from here
===================================

Closed since April 2021, there’s no sign that Plymouth commuter rail station will ever re-open.

by [Fred Thys - Independent Staff](https://www.plymouthindependent.org/author/fred-thys-independent-staff/) 11/21/202311/21/2023

![Image 2](https://www.plymouthindependent.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/Plymouth-MBTA-1200x1200.jpg)

The deserted MBTA commuter rail stop at Cordage Park in North Plymouth features a poster for 2019-2020 Plymouth activities. Credit: (Photo by Mark Pothier)

The platforms at the Plymouth MBTA commuter rail station offer a spectacular water view, access to a rail trail, and parking.

One thing they do not offer: trains.

The adjacent Cordage Park development’s [website](https://www.cordagecc.com/property#site) still touts “an MBTA station, providing direct access to Boston, conveniently on-site.”

But the two college campuses and offices and restaurants of the Cordage development and the 303 Harborwalk apartments are still T-less, more than two-and-a-half years after it closed.

“The reason it was all built was because of the train station,” State Rep. Matthew Muratore, R-Plymouth, said of the large apartment complex.

Service at the station began in 1997, Lisa Battiston, a spokesperson for the MBTA, said, with the restoration of the long dormant Old Colony commuter rail line.

A [schedule](https://www.dbperry.net/MBTA/old_colony/old_colony_2007-01-01.pdf) from 2007 shows that four trains operated in each direction between Plymouth and Boston’s South Station on weekdays. None ran during rush hour. On weekends, three trains operated daily.

The station was [one of 6 commuter rail stations](https://www.mbta.com/service-changes/spring-2021-service-changes) to close in April 2021, during the COVID-19 pandemic, and has remained closed since.

Muratore said that until then, he and other members of the Plymouth delegation in the state Legislature had pressed to keep the station open, even though its limited schedule yielded about a dozen passengers per train. The North Plymouth location and limited parking didn’t help.

Thank you to our sponsors. [Become a sponsor](https://www.plymouthindependent.org/sponsorships/).

“So when COVID came and they decided to shut it, we were all very concerned about that,” Muratore said. “Once you close a station, it’s a lot harder to open it back up. We really need to get that station opened with a better schedule because of all the growth that’s not just in that area, but the town of Plymouth itself.”

![Image 3](https://www.plymouthindependent.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/Plymouth-MBTA-Closed.jpg)

The sign may say that the Plymouth commuter rail station is temporarily closed, but there’s no sign that it will reopen anytime soon. Credit: (Photo by Mark Pothier)

Currently, the end of the line is in Kingston, less than three miles away, a station with easy access to Route 3 and plenty of parking spaces.

“It doesn’t bother me,” Lisa Golz said as she got off the 5:33 p.m. train from Boston before heading to her car for the short drive home to Court Street in Plymouth. Besides, she said, given the scarcity of trains to Plymouth when they did run, she still had to drive to Kingston because of her schedule.

“There were no times for commuters,” she said of the pre-pandemic service.

Passenger Victoria J., who declined to give her full last name, had to order an Uber from the Kingston station to meet a friend who had just moved to Cordage Park. “I don’t get to walk to her apartment,” she said.

Muratore said MBTA management has assured the Plymouth delegation that it will meet with them over the next few months to discuss the status of the Plymouth station.

Battiston said the meeting is in the process of being scheduled.

_Fred Thys can be reached at [fred@plymouthindependent.org](mailto:fred@plymouthindependent.org)._

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia
Massachusetts Coastal Railroad
Overview
HeadquartersTaunton, Massachusetts
Reporting markMC
LocaleMassachusetts
Dates of operation2007–present
PredecessorBay Colony Railroad
Technical
Track gauge4 ft 8+1⁄2 in (1,435 mm) standard gauge
Length135 Miles
Other
Websitemasscoastal.com
The **Massachusetts Coastal Railroad** ([reporting mark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reporting_mark "Reporting mark") **MC**) is a [Class III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Railroad_classes "Railroad classes") railroad serving south-eastern Massachusetts. The railroad maintains track from Hyannis to Framingham, operating over 135 miles of track between Hyannis and Fall River/New Bedford.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Coastal_Railroad#cite_note-1) The railroad is the successor operator of portions of the [Bay Colony Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bay_Colony_Railroad "Bay Colony Railroad"). On December 31, 2007, the contract to operate the freight railroad lines owned by the Commonwealth of [Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts "Massachusetts") administered by the Executive Office of Transportation (EOT) expired. These railroad lines included the [Cape Main Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Cod_Railroad "Cape Cod Railroad"), as well as several shorter lines both on Cape Cod and in Southeastern Massachusetts. The new contract was awarded to a new company, the Massachusetts Coastal Railroad, which took over on January 1, 2008. At that time, the Bay Colony ceased operations on those lines, but continues to operate in other areas of the Commonwealth, including on the [Watuppa Branch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Watuppa_Branch "Watuppa Branch") in Dartmouth and Westport, and the [Millis Branch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Millis_Branch "Millis Branch") in Millis.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Coastal_Railroad#cite_note-Trains-2) On November 16, 2023, the railroad indicated that it would be purchasing the Watuppa Branch and Millis Branch from the Bay Colony and taking over operations on the lines.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Coastal_Railroad#cite_note-3)[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Coastal_Railroad#cite_note-4) The purchase of the Millis Branch was initially rejected by the [Surface Transportation Board](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface_Transportation_Board "Surface Transportation Board") due to uncertainty about the status of the line,[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Coastal_Railroad#cite_note-5) but the line's operations were ultimately taken over Massachusetts Coastal later that year. The Massachusetts Coastal Railroad is headquartered in [Taunton, Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taunton,_Massachusetts "Taunton, Massachusetts").[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Coastal_Railroad#cite_note-6) [![Image 2](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4f/Mass_Coastal_train_on_east_side_of_Canal%2C_June_2014.jpg/250px-Mass_Coastal_train_on_east_side_of_Canal%2C_June_2014.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Mass_Coastal_train_on_east_side_of_Canal,_June_2014.jpg) A Mass Coastal trash train running along the Cape Cod Canal in 2014 The railroad operates the "trash train" hauling refuse from the [Upper Cape Regional Transfer Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upper_Cape_Regional_Transfer_Station "Upper Cape Regional Transfer Station") in [Falmouth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Falmouth,_Massachusetts "Falmouth, Massachusetts") and the Yarmouth-Barnstable Regional Transfer Station in [Yarmouth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yarmouth,_Massachusetts "Yarmouth, Massachusetts") to the [Southeastern Massachusetts Resource Recovery Facility](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Massachusetts_Resource_Recovery_Facility "Southeastern Massachusetts Resource Recovery Facility"), a [waste-to-energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waste-to-energy "Waste-to-energy") plant in [Rochester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rochester,_Massachusetts "Rochester, Massachusetts"), MA, as did its predecessor. The operations occur entirely along the [Cape Main Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Main_Line "Cape Main Line"), including the spur to Falmouth. However, Massachusetts Coastal operates the train under the new name, "Energy Train" using 20 former [Canadian Pacific](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_Pacific "Canadian Pacific") bath tub coal [hopper cars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hopper_car "Hopper car") rebuilt into "Energy" cars. These "Energy Cars" are numbered 1000–1019. These cars are painted in a Pullman green scheme with a black band. The first 6 cars were fully painted with "MASS COASTAL" lettering, and "ENERGY TRAIN" written along the sides and gold stripes. The remaining 14 cars are in an abbreviated scheme with no lettering or stripes. This was done to speed up the delivery process. As of January 2015, the Energy Train operates Monday through Friday in the morning and afternoon. [![Image 3: Hyannis Yard Railfan Day 2023](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c2/Railfan_Day_2023_Yard.jpg/250px-Railfan_Day_2023_Yard.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Railfan_Day_2023_Yard.jpg) Massachusetts Coastal Railroad, MBTA, and Cape Cod Central Railroad equipment at Hyannis in August 2023 In addition to the energy train, Mass Coastal offers general freight transport for companies based on Cape Cod and the south coast, specifically along the [Cape Main](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Main_Line "Cape Main Line"), [Middleboro Secondary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middleboro_Secondary "Middleboro Secondary"), [New Bedford Subdivision](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Bedford_Subdivision "New Bedford Subdivision"), [Fall River Secondary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River_Secondary "Fall River Secondary"), and the [Dean Street Industrial Track](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dighton_and_Somerset_Railroad "Dighton and Somerset Railroad") (the latter of which is located in [Taunton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taunton,_Massachusetts "Taunton, Massachusetts")). Interchanges are done with CSX in Middleboro several times a week, to allow for long-distance shipping to and from the region. Operations in Fall River, New Bedford, and Taunton can be seen some days Monday through Friday. Mass Coastal does not operate freight trains on Sundays or holidays unless needed. The [Cape Cod Central Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Cod_Central_Railroad "Cape Cod Central Railroad") is owned by the same parent company, and operates passenger trains as a [heritage railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heritage_railroad "Heritage railroad"). A plan to start "Mass Coastal" [commuter rail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commuter_rail "Commuter rail") service between Middleborough and Buzzards Bay or Sandwich in 2010[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Coastal_Railroad#cite_note-7) has not been implemented as of 2023, but the seasonal [CapeFLYER](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CapeFLYER "CapeFLYER") train started running to Hyannis in the summer of 2013. In 2012, Chicago-based [Iowa Pacific Holdings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iowa_Pacific_Holdings "Iowa Pacific Holdings") acquired Cape Rail, Inc and its subsidiaries Mass Coastal and Cape Cod Central.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Coastal_Railroad#cite_note-iowapacificacquires-8) After Iowa Pacific collapsed in 2020, MassCoastal and Cape Cod Central were bought by P. Christopher Podgurski, a Cape Cod native. Mass Coastal took over CSX tracks from Taunton, MA to Fall River and New Bedford, MA.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Coastal_Railroad#cite_note-Cape_Cod_Times-9) The railroad continues to operate track south from the connection with CSX at Cotley Junction in Taunton to both New Bedford and Fall River. In late 2023, the last of Bay Colony's active lines (the [Watuppa branch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Watuppa_branch "Watuppa branch") and the [Millis Branch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Millis_Branch "Millis Branch")) were purchased by Massachusetts Coastal.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Coastal_Railroad#cite_note-MassCoastal-10) The STB approved the Millis Branch transfer in June 2024 after a delay due to uncertainty about the status of the line.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Coastal_Railroad#cite_note-11) 1. **[^](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Coastal_Railroad#cite_ref-1)** ["About Mass Coastal Railroad | Rail Freight"](https://masscoastal.com/about/). _masscoastal.com_. [Kalmbach Publishing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalmbach_Publishing "Kalmbach Publishing"). October 8, 2007. From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia
Bay Colony Railroad

Bay Colony Railroad locomotive in Medfield, Massachusetts, in 2017

Overview
HeadquartersBraintree, Massachusetts
Reporting markBCLR
LocaleMassachusetts
Dates of operation1982–2023
PredecessorConrail
SuccessorMassachusetts Coastal Railroad
Technical
Track gauge4 ft 8+1⁄2 in (1,435 mm) standard gauge
Length34 miles (55 km)
Other
Websitewww.baycolonyrailroad.com
The **Bay Colony Railroad** ([reporting mark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reporting_mark "Reporting mark") **BCLR**) was a [shortline railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shortline_railroad "Shortline railroad") (STB [Class III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Class_iii_railroad "Class iii railroad")) operating in [Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts "Massachusetts"). Formerly operating along most of the south coast region (including all lines on [Cape Cod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Cod "Cape Cod")), Bay Colony's final operations ceased in late 2023, when the only two remaining lines (a roughly six-mile stretch of track between [New Bedford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Bedford,_Massachusetts "New Bedford, Massachusetts") and [Westport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westport,_Massachusetts "Westport, Massachusetts"), referred to as the [Watuppa Branch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Watuppa_Branch "Watuppa Branch"), as well as a section of the [Millis Branch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Millis_Branch "Millis Branch") from Medfield Junction to Millis) were purchased by [Massachusetts Coastal Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Coastal_Railroad "Massachusetts Coastal Railroad"). In addition to moving freight for its customers, Bay Colony also performed [AAR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_of_American_Railroads "Association of American Railroads")\-certified repairs on rolling stock and contract track construction projects for other railroads. It had a sister railroad, the [Seminole Gulf Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seminole_Gulf_Railway "Seminole Gulf Railway"), which is based out of [Fort Myers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Myers "Fort Myers"), [Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida "Florida"). [![Image 3](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/b/b6/BCLR_Original_Logo.svg/250px-BCLR_Original_Logo.svg.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:BCLR_Original_Logo.svg) Bay Colony Railroad's original logo, marked on boxcar livery up through the mid-nineties The Bay Colony railroad was chartered on March 31, 1977, with the intent of taking over freight service on former New Haven lines from [Conrail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conrail "Conrail"), which was planning to abandon service.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bay_Colony_Railroad#cite_note-1) The lines were purchased by the state government, and Bay Colony took over all freight operations on the lines on June 12, 1982 with a 25-year contract.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bay_Colony_Railroad#cite_note-Trains-2) Bay Colony expressed interest in purchasing the [Belfast and Moosehead Lake Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belfast_and_Moosehead_Lake_Railroad_/(1871%E2%80%932007/) "Belfast and Moosehead Lake Railroad (1871–2007)") in 1983.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bay_Colony_Railroad#cite_note-3) The contract for the railroad lines owned by the Commonwealth of Massachusetts administered by the Executive Office of Transportation (EOT), which included the Cape Cod main expired on December 31, 2007. It was awarded to a new company, the [Massachusetts Coastal Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Coastal_Railroad "Massachusetts Coastal Railroad"), which took over on January 1, 2008. At that time the Bay Colony ceased operation on those lines, but continued to maintain operations in other areas of the state, namely the Millis branch (until 2018) and the Watuppa branch.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bay_Colony_Railroad#cite_note-Trains-2) The Bay Colony Railroad maintained its headquartered in [Braintree, Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Braintree,_Massachusetts "Braintree, Massachusetts"), and owned 6 miles (9.7 km) of active trackage within Massachusetts.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bay_Colony_Railroad#cite_note-:0-4) Bay Colony continued operations along the [Millis Branch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Millis_Branch "Millis Branch"), a roughly eight-mile segment of track between [Needham Junction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Needham_Junction "Needham Junction") and the former [Millis station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Millis_station "Millis station"). This line interchanged with CSX at Medfield. The last train between Needham and Medfield ran in 2006, and this section was abandoned in 2008.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bay_Colony_Railroad#cite_note-5) Owned by the [MBTA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Bay_Transportation_Authority "Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority"), this section became the [Bay Colony Rail Trail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bay_Colony_Rail_Trail "Bay Colony Rail Trail"). By May 2018, Bay Colony had ceased regular operations of this branch from Millis to Medfield following the closure of GAF Roofing, the biggest customer on the line.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bay_Colony_Railroad#cite_note-:0-4) Bay Colony also operated along the [Watuppa Branch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Watuppa_Branch "Watuppa Branch") (also referred to as the North Dartmouth Industrial Track), a roughly six-mile stretch of track in the south coast of the state. The branch diverges from the [New Bedford Secondary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Bedford_Secondary "New Bedford Secondary") and passes through the town of [Dartmouth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dartmouth,_Massachusetts "Dartmouth, Massachusetts") before terminating in Westport. Interchange was with Mass Coastal in New Bedford.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bay_Colony_Railroad#cite_note-:0-4) In November 2023, Mass Coastal indicated that it had agreed to purchase the Millis Branch and Watuppa Branch from Bay Colony and operate the lines, ending all remaining operations by the Bay Colony.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bay_Colony_Railroad#cite_note-6)[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bay_Colony_Railroad#cite_note-7) However, on December 15, the [Surface Transportation Board](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface_Transportation_Board "Surface Transportation Board") (STB) rejected the transfer of Millis Branch operations due to uncertainty about the status of the line.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bay_Colony_Railroad#cite_note-8) Mass Coastal announced the purchase of the Bay Colony was final in February 2024, excluding the Millis Branch which remained held up by legal issues.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bay_Colony_Railroad#cite_note-9) The STB approved the Millis Branch transfer in June 2024.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bay_Colony_Railroad#cite_note-10) * [Cape Cod Canal Railroad Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Cod_Canal_Railroad_Bridge "Cape Cod Canal Railroad Bridge") 1. **[^](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bay_Colony_Railroad#cite_ref-1)** ["about bay colony"](https://web.archive.org/web/20030407171038/http://www.baycolonyrr.com/about%20bay%20colony.htm). Operating Lines
===============

### When the First and Last Miles are the Most Important

Mass Coastal Railroad holds the freight rights and operates on 135 miles of track throughout Massachusetts. From the Southeast Mass Lines on Cape Cod to the Millis Branch Line, Mass Coastal holds trackage to serve our customers across the Commonwealth. Mass Coastal interchanges daily with our Class 1 partner CSX at two locations – Taunton and Middleboro. Through our partnership with CSX, shippers can ship products and materials to and from any location in the United States, Canada, and Mexico.

### Southeast Mass Lines

The Southeast Mass Lines include the Cape Main line, stretching from Middleboro to Hyannis and South Yarmouth, and the Falmouth Secondary line from Buzzards Bay to North Falmouth and Otis Air Force Base.

### South Coast Lines

The South Coast Lines include tracks from Taunton/Myricks to Fall River and New Bedford. Also includes the Watuppa Branch Line to Dartmouth/Westport.

### Kingston Line

The Kingston Line interchanges at Braintree, and stretches to Kingston and Plymouth. Mass Coastal holds the freight rights on this MBTA operated line.

### Millis Line

The Millis Line is a Mass Coastal branch line from Medfield Junction to Millis, and connects to the Framingham Secondary.

**Date** **ArticleType** 2/9/2024 3:15:14 PM General

### Mass Coastal Railroad Acquires Bay Colony Railroad

Massachusetts Coastal Railroad (MCRR) announced its acquisition of the assets of the Bay Colony Railroad (BCLR) today. Under the agreement, MCRR will acquire the permanent freight easement to 35 Miles of track currently operated by Bay Colony. In doing so MCRR expands to operate 132 route miles of track and becomes the custodian of an additional 44 miles of railroad track owned by MASSDOT.

“This is an important step forward for efficient, environmentally friendly freight rail service in Massachusetts,” said Chris Podgurski, President and CEO of MCRR. “Hauling freight by rail instead of by truck not only reduces congestion on our roads, but it also significantly reduces greenhouse gases which helps to fight global warming.”

Massachusetts Coastal Railroad partners with the Massachusetts Department of Transportation Rail Unit, the MBTA and the railroad’s Class 1 partner CSXT Transportation to provide a crucial rail connection to the National Rail Network that extends into Canada and Mexico.

“Bay Colony currently serves three customers in Dartmouth and Westport, positioning us to acquire some additional rail users, as well,” Podgurski added. “The Bay Colony properties are a welcome addition to our existing 97 miles of track and will enhance our freight shipping capabilities on behalf of Massachusetts businesses and residents.”

“This expansion is a tribute to our skilled employees,” he continued. “The Mass Coastal team members are crucial to the day-to-day operations of the railroad, and this couldn’t happen without them.”

Bay Colony has owned and managed the short line railroad in Southeastern Massachusetts since 1982. Going forward, MCRR will manage the railroad’s daily operations. MCRR applied to the federal Surface Transportation Board for approval for of the transaction, which was granted in December. MASSDOT, which owns the tracks that are leased by the railroads, was consulted throughout the process.

MCRR has continued to advocate for the preservation and expansion of rail transit in Massachusetts. Their existing rail lines are used for the Cape Flyer, Cape Cod’s Polar Express Train and industrial freight shipping for multiple Cape Cod municipalities and private businesses.

About Mass Coastal Railroad: Since 2008, the Mass Coastal Railroad has provided integrated rail freight and logistics services to businesses and industries throughout the South Coast of Massachusetts and Southern New England since 2008. Our railroad operates a network of lines now totaling almost 176 miles of track stretching from Framingham to the Southcoast of Fall River & New Bedford to Hyannis. Learn more at [masscoastal.com.](https://l.facebook.com/l.php?u=http%3A%2F%2Fmasscoastal.com%2F%3Ffbclid%3DIwAR3_TLtuu3cFWFIdTY9Fb9cFmyjLLO0tXOlKvQ4ESJ86DKLZeuDNoUGpHdw&h=AT2P_0cwF_ozGEXEXZqHr8XDZOHVIXlv5qXvrh4S3nCJNvq_n3HAXh0JP4-Vo6IalG6tFy6qf1Yog_D4da4SUBA7GF3tg1dMyLkS9LgNyTKvzZ7q4QLJAPSA4dQTMv-AfQ&__tn__=-UK-R&c%5b0%5d=AT3Au7soyKdmCi8N4Vttd5KhfKLvU1nrZEcjz6BktLXezzHdixPkLT6e5U4gEwCdAusxNUh5D-yI88lC27FKQBL5a0JL78BjDAouv3z3D3SlT05FeImgeDmIfiZ0CKNeFR77VPD2NicerWB84QURqAjoM_S06iicqrWckhV6X9Bwy9Bs2H3XzQ41M5UGTtMZu4AVAA)

Vineyard Railroad [![Image 11](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cc/Old_Colony_RR_1883.jpg/250px-Old_Colony_RR_1883.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Old_Colony_RR_1883.jpg) Share of the Old Colony Railroad Company, issued April 27, 1883 The **Old Colony Railroad** (OC) was a major [railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Railroad "Railroad") system, mainly covering southeastern [Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts "Massachusetts") and parts of [Rhode Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhode_Island "Rhode Island"), which operated from 1845 to 1893. Old Colony trains ran from [Boston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston "Boston") to points such as [Plymouth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plymouth,_Massachusetts "Plymouth, Massachusetts"), [Fall River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River,_Massachusetts "Fall River, Massachusetts"), [New Bedford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Bedford "New Bedford"), [Newport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newport,_Rhode_Island "Newport, Rhode Island"), [Providence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Providence,_Rhode_Island "Providence, Rhode Island"), [Fitchburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fitchburg,_Massachusetts "Fitchburg, Massachusetts"), [Lowell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lowell,_Massachusetts "Lowell, Massachusetts") and [Cape Cod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Cod "Cape Cod"). For many years the Old Colony Railroad Company also operated steamboat and ferry lines, including those of the [Fall River Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River_Line "Fall River Line") with express train service from Boston to its wharf in Fall River where passengers boarded luxury liners to New York City. The company also briefly operated a [railroad line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha%27s_Vineyard_Railroad "Martha's Vineyard Railroad") on [Martha's Vineyard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha%27s_Vineyard "Martha's Vineyard"), as well as the freight-only [Union Freight Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_Freight_Railroad "Union Freight Railroad") in Boston. The OC was named after the "Old Colony", the nickname for the [Plymouth Colony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plymouth_Colony "Plymouth Colony"). From 1845 to 1893, the OC network grew extensively largely through a series of [mergers and acquisitions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mergers_and_acquisitions "Mergers and acquisitions") with other established railroads, until it was itself acquired by the [New York, New Haven and Hartford Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York,_New_Haven_and_Hartford_Railroad "New York, New Haven and Hartford Railroad") under a lease agreement on March 1, 1893, for its entire 617-mile (993 km) network.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Colony_Railroad#cite_note-2) After this date, all trains, lines, and stations became known as the "Old Colony Division" of the huge "New Haven" system. During this period, the New York, New Haven and Hartford Railroad enjoyed a virtual monopoly on all passenger and freight rail service in southern [New England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_England "New England"). Passenger service on the New Haven's Old Colony Division ended in 1959, except for the [main line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northeast_Corridor "Northeast Corridor") between Boston and Providence and other ex-[Boston and Providence Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_and_Providence_Railroad "Boston and Providence Railroad") lines. Several lines have been restored to passenger service: the [Plymouth/Kingston Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plymouth/Kingston_Line "Plymouth/Kingston Line") and [Middleborough/Lakeville Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middleborough/Lakeville_Line "Middleborough/Lakeville Line") in 1997, and the [Greenbush Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenbush_Line "Greenbush Line") in 2007. The [South Coast Rail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail "South Coast Rail") project extended the Middleborough/Lakeville line in 2025 as the [Fall River/New Bedford Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line "Fall River/New Bedford Line"). Other parts of the former OC system continue to be used for freight service by [CSX Transportation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CSX_Transportation "CSX Transportation") and other [short line railroads](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Short_line_railroads "Short line railroads"), including the [Massachusetts Coastal Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Coastal_Railroad "Massachusetts Coastal Railroad") which operates on Cape Cod and in southeastern Massachusetts. Parts of the former OC on Cape Cod are also still used to operate the [Cape Cod Central Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Cod_Central_Railroad "Cape Cod Central Railroad") tourist train from [Hyannis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyannis,_Massachusetts "Hyannis, Massachusetts") to [Buzzards Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buzzards_Bay,_Massachusetts "Buzzards Bay, Massachusetts") during the summer and fall months. Another tourist railroad, the [Old Colony and Newport Scenic Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Colony_and_Newport_Scenic_Railway "Old Colony and Newport Scenic Railway") operates on part of the former OC from Newport on [Aquidneck Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aquidneck_Island "Aquidneck Island"). Several abandoned portions of the OC have been converted into multi-use [rail trails](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_trail "Rail trail"). These include the [East Bay Bike Path](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Bay_Bike_Path "East Bay Bike Path") in [Rhode Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhode_Island "Rhode Island"),[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Colony_Railroad#cite_note-3) as well as others in Lowell, [Mansfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mansfield,_Massachusetts "Mansfield, Massachusetts"), [Fairhaven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fairhaven,_Massachusetts "Fairhaven, Massachusetts"), and the [Cape Cod Rail Trail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Cod_Rail_Trail "Cape Cod Rail Trail") on Cape Cod.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Colony_Railroad#cite_note-4) ### Old Colony Railroad (1844–1854) \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Old_Colony_Railroad&action=edit§ion=2 "Edit section: Old Colony Railroad (1844–1854)")\] By the early 1840s, the city of [Boston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston "Boston") had six major rail lines connecting it with other places including [Lowell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lowell,_Massachusetts "Lowell, Massachusetts"), [Maine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maine "Maine"), [Fitchburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fitchburg,_Massachusetts "Fitchburg, Massachusetts"), and [Salem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salem,_Massachusetts "Salem, Massachusetts") to the north, [Worcester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Worcester,_Massachusetts "Worcester, Massachusetts") to the west and [Providence, Rhode Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Providence,_Rhode_Island "Providence, Rhode Island") to the southwest. The southeastern part of [Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts "Massachusetts") had yet to be served by a rail link to Boston. On March 16, 1844, the Old Colony Railroad Corporation was formed to provide a rail connection between Boston and [Plymouth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plymouth,_Massachusetts "Plymouth, Massachusetts"). Construction of the line began in [South Boston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Boston,_Massachusetts "South Boston, Massachusetts") in June 1844 and the 36.8-mile (59.2 km) line opened to Plymouth on November 10, 1845. The extension from South Boston to the newly completed Kneeland Street Station in Boston opened on June 19, 1847. Kneeland Street also served as the headquarters for the OC until the 1893 consolidation. There had previously been an Old Colony Railroad formed in 1838 for a line between [Taunton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taunton,_Massachusetts "Taunton, Massachusetts") and [New Bedford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Bedford "New Bedford"), but the name was changed to the [New Bedford and Taunton Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Bedford_and_Taunton_Railroad "New Bedford and Taunton Railroad") in 1839 before service began in 1840. This line would later become part of OC in 1879. John Sever of [Kingston, Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston,_Massachusetts "Kingston, Massachusetts"), served as the first president of the Old Colony Railroad Corporation from 1844-1845. [Nathan Carruth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nathan_Carruth "Nathan Carruth") served as the second president of the corporation from 1845 to 1848. Carruth was a successful businessman and enthusiastic supporter of the expansion of railroads in Massachusetts and elsewhere in [New England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_England "New England"). With the opening of the Old Colony line through [Dorchester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorchester,_Massachusetts "Dorchester, Massachusetts") in 1845, Carruth became actively involved in the development of the area.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Colony_Railroad#cite_note-5) He built an estate on the east side of Dorchester Avenue called Beechmont/Beaumont which would become one of the first railroad suburbs in America.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Colony_Railroad#cite_note-6) All OC locomotives were named until 1884, after which they were simply numbered. Among the early engines were the _Mayflower_, _Governor Carver_, _Governor Bradford_, and _Miles Standish_. The new railroad company also built the _Samoset Hotel_ near the end of its line in Plymouth.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Colony_Railroad#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFisher191913-7) In 1847, the OC completed a short 6.2-mile (10.0 km) connector line from its main line at [Whitman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whitman,_Massachusetts "Whitman, Massachusetts") to the [Fall River Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River_Railroad_/(1846/) "Fall River Railroad (1846)") line at Bridgewater Junction. On April 1, 1849, OC signed a lease of the [South Shore Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Shore_Railroad "South Shore Railroad") for a period of five years. By 1851, traffic on the line had increased enough to warrant the opening of a second track running between Boston and [South Braintree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Braintree "South Braintree"). ### Old Colony and Fall River Railroad (1854–1863) \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Old_Colony_Railroad&action=edit§ion=3 "Edit section: Old Colony and Fall River Railroad (1854–1863)")\] The OC and Fall River Railroad merged with a joint stock vote on June 20, 1854, forming the _Old Colony and Fall River Railroad Company_,[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Colony_Railroad#cite_note-8) which provided a two-pronged line from Boston to Plymouth and Boston to [Fall River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River,_Massachusetts "Fall River, Massachusetts"), splitting at South Braintree. Alexander Holmes from [Kingston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston,_Massachusetts "Kingston, Massachusetts") served as company president during this period, from 1854 to 1866. The Fall River Railroad had been formed on August 8, 1845, with the consolidation of three companies; the [Fall River Branch Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River_Branch_Railroad "Fall River Branch Railroad"), the Randolph and Bridgewater Railroad and the Middleborough Railroad. The Fall River Railroad was led by [Richard Borden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Borden "Richard Borden"), a prominent Fall River mill owner who wanted a direct route to Boston that did not require the use of the [Boston and Providence Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_and_Providence_Railroad "Boston and Providence Railroad") lines. The line from South Braintree to [Myricks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Myricks,_Massachusetts "Myricks, Massachusetts") in the town of [Berkley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berkley,_Massachusetts "Berkley, Massachusetts") opened on December 16, 1846, as an extension of the Fall River Branch Railroad – which had been completed in 1845. On May 19, 1847, the first "boat train" left the OC's Kneeland Street Station in Boston bound for Fall River, where passengers would board a steamship for New York City. Over the years, the _Old Colony Steamboat Express_ train would become the most famous line of the Old Colony Railroad, with the finest and most up-to-date engines, cars and attention to detail. In 1863 the Old Colony and Fall River Railroad acquired the [Dorchester and Milton Branch Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorchester_and_Milton_Branch_Railroad "Dorchester and Milton Branch Railroad") Company, which it had been leasing since 1848. ### Old Colony and Newport Railway (1863–1872) \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Old_Colony_Railroad&action=edit§ion=4 "Edit section: Old Colony and Newport Railway (1863–1872)")\] The _Old Colony and Newport Railway_ was formed in July 1863 when the Old Colony and Fall River Railroad merged with the Newport and Fall River Railroad, which had been incorporated in 1846 to build a road from [Newport, Rhode Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newport,_Rhode_Island "Newport, Rhode Island") to the Massachusetts state line at Fall River. However, the road from Fall River to the Rhode Island state line was not authorized by the [Commonwealth of Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_of_Massachusetts "Commonwealth of Massachusetts") until 1860. The newly formed and renamed _Old Colony and Newport Railway Company_ completed the final section of the line from Fall River to Newport which finally opened for service on February 5, 1864. In 1865, the Old Colony and Newport Railway Company acquired the [Dighton and Somerset Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dighton_and_Somerset_Railroad "Dighton and Somerset Railroad"). It completed a new, more direct route between Fall River and Boston via South Braintree on September 24, 1866. Part of the new route was over the [Easton Branch Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Easton_Branch_Railroad&action=edit&redlink=1 "Easton Branch Railroad (page does not exist)") between [Stoughton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stoughton,_Massachusetts "Stoughton, Massachusetts") and [North Easton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Easton,_Massachusetts "North Easton, Massachusetts"). In 1871 the Old Colony purchased the Easton Branch. A portion of the old [Granite Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granite_Railway "Granite Railway") line was acquired in 1870 and later extended to form a loop through [West Quincy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Quincy,_Massachusetts "West Quincy, Massachusetts") off the original Plymouth line. In 1872, the Old Colony & Newport Railway Corporation built the [Shawmut Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Shawmut_Railroad&action=edit&redlink=1 "Shawmut Railroad (page does not exist)") as a connection between the [Dorchester and Milton Branch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorchester_and_Milton_Branch_Railroad "Dorchester and Milton Branch Railroad") and the main line to Boston. ### Old Colony Railroad (1872–1893) \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Old_Colony_Railroad&action=edit§ion=5 "Edit section: Old Colony Railroad (1872–1893)")\] The Old Colony and Newport Railway merged with the [Cape Cod Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Cod_Railroad "Cape Cod Railroad") on May 1, 1872, and the two companies were consolidated on October 1, forming a new _Old Colony Railroad Company_ under the leadership of [Onslow Stearns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Onslow_Stearns "Onslow Stearns"), who served as president of the company from 1866 to 1877. The 1872 merger formed a system with three main branches; Boston to Plymouth, South Braintree to Fall River and Newport, and a third splitting from the Newport branch at [Middleborough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middleborough,_Massachusetts "Middleborough, Massachusetts") to [Hyannis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyannis,_Massachusetts "Hyannis, Massachusetts"). At this point, the newly acquired lines became known as the Cape Cod Division, with a new superintendent's office located at Hyannis. The [Cape Cod Railroad Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Cod_Railroad "Cape Cod Railroad") had been established in 1846 as the [Cape Cod Branch Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Cod_Branch_Railroad "Cape Cod Branch Railroad") with a line off the Fall River Railroad from Middleborough to [Sandwich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sandwich,_Massachusetts "Sandwich, Massachusetts") opening in 1848. Among the proponents of the Cape Cod Branch Railroad was Richard Borden of Fall River, who saw the new line as an opportunity to bring more traffic and business through his hometown.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Colony_Railroad#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFisher1919146-9)In 1853, the extension of the line to Hyannis was started, reaching [West Barnstable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Barnstable,_Massachusetts "West Barnstable, Massachusetts") on December 22, 1853. On February 22, 1854, the Cape Cod Branch Railroad was renamed the Cape Cod Railroad Company. In the spring of 1854, construction continued, with the railroad reaching [Barnstable village](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barnstable_/(village/),_Massachusetts "Barnstable (village), Massachusetts") on May 8, [Yarmouth Port](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yarmouth_Port,_Massachusetts "Yarmouth Port, Massachusetts") on May 19, and finally Hyannis on July 8, 1854. Connecting [steamboat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steamboat "Steamboat") service to [Nantucket](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nantucket,_Massachusetts "Nantucket, Massachusetts") commenced from Hyannis in late September and would continue until 1872, when the railroad branch to [Woods Hole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woods_Hole "Woods Hole") was opened. The [Cape Cod Central Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Cod_Central_Railroad "Cape Cod Central Railroad") was incorporated in 1861 as a branch from the Cape Cod Railroad, running from [Yarmouth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yarmouth,_Massachusetts "Yarmouth, Massachusetts") east and northeast to [Orleans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orleans,_Massachusetts "Orleans, Massachusetts"), and opening in 1865. The Cape Cod Central was purchased by the Cape Cod Railroad April 21, 1868, and the two railroads were consolidated on July 28, 1868. The newly formed Old Colony Railroad extended the line to [Provincetown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Provincetown,_Massachusetts "Provincetown, Massachusetts"), at the very tip of Cape Cod, opening on July 23, 1873. In 1874, Old Colony founded the [Martha's Vineyard Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha%27s_Vineyard_Railroad "Martha's Vineyard Railroad"), built across nine miles (14.5 km) on sand of the island of [Martha's Vineyard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha%27s_Vineyard "Martha's Vineyard"), running from the [Oak Bluffs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oak_Bluffs "Oak Bluffs") steamer wharf to Mattakeeset Lodge in [Katama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Katama "Katama"), [Edgartown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edgartown "Edgartown"). The locomotive _Active_ (later renamed the _South Beach_) was the sole operating train. This branch existed until 1896.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Colony_Railroad#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHough1936263-10) The Old Colony Railroad acquired the [Middleborough and Taunton Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middleborough_and_Taunton_Railroad "Middleborough and Taunton Railroad") in 1874 and the [South Shore Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Shore_Railroad "South Shore Railroad") in 1877, which it had once leased until 1854. A year later in 1878 it acquired the [Duxbury and Cohasset Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duxbury_and_Cohasset_Railroad "Duxbury and Cohasset Railroad") which gave the Old Colony a connection with its original 1845 main line at [Kingston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston,_Massachusetts "Kingston, Massachusetts"). Beginning in 1874, the Old Colony operated the "South Shore, Duxbury and Cohasset and Plymouth Express" between Boston and Plymouth on this line.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Colony_Railroad#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFisher191946-11) In 1875, the Old Colony Railroad began operating the [Fall River, Warren and Providence Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River,_Warren_and_Providence_Railroad "Fall River, Warren and Providence Railroad"), which had been formed in 1863 as a merger between the Warren and Fall River and Fall River and Warren Railroad Companies. The Old Colony would later acquire this line outright in 1892. In 1879, the Old Colony Railroad greatly expanded its network into Central Massachusetts by leasing the [Boston, Clinton, Fitchburg and New Bedford Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston,_Clinton,_Fitchburg_and_New_Bedford_Railroad "Boston, Clinton, Fitchburg and New Bedford Railroad") for 999 years, then purchasing it outright in 1883. The acquisition of this line provided important connections for the Old Colony, such as with the [Boston and Providence Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_and_Providence_Railroad "Boston and Providence Railroad") at [Mansfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mansfield,_Massachusetts "Mansfield, Massachusetts"), the [Boston and Albany Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_and_Albany_Railroad "Boston and Albany Railroad") at [South Framingham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Framingham,_Massachusetts "South Framingham, Massachusetts") and the [Fitchburg Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fitchburg_Railroad "Fitchburg Railroad") at [Fitchburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fitchburg,_Massachusetts "Fitchburg, Massachusetts"), among others. This deal also gave the Old Colony Railroad direct access to the important industrial port of New Bedford. Upon this acquisition, the lines of the former [Boston, Clinton and Fitchburg Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston,_Clinton_and_Fitchburg_Railroad "Boston, Clinton and Fitchburg Railroad") became known as the Old Colony's "Northern Division", with headquarters in Fitchburg, while the older OCRR lines became known as the "Central Division" with headquarters in Boston. In 1882 the Old Colony Railroad signed a 99-year lease on a line between Fall River and New Bedford through the towns of [Dartmouth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dartmouth,_Massachusetts "Dartmouth, Massachusetts") and [Westport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westport,_Massachusetts "Westport, Massachusetts") owned by the [Fall River Railroad (1874)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River_Railroad_/(1874/) "Fall River Railroad (1874)") – not to be confused with its [1846 namesake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River_Railroad_/(1846/) "Fall River Railroad (1846)"). In 1886 the Old Colony Railroad acquired the [Lowell and Framingham Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lowell_and_Framingham_Railroad "Lowell and Framingham Railroad"), which before 1871 had been known as the [Framingham and Lowell Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Framingham_and_Lowell_Railroad "Framingham and Lowell Railroad"). In 1887 the Old Colony Railroad acquired the [Hanover Branch Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hanover_Branch_Railroad_/(Massachusetts/) "Hanover Branch Railroad (Massachusetts)"). On April 1, 1888, the Old Colony Railroad signed a 99-year lease agreement the [Nantasket Beach Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nantasket_Beach_Railroad "Nantasket Beach Railroad") with service to [Hull](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hull,_Massachusetts "Hull, Massachusetts"). Several days later, on April 7, 1888 the OCRR signed a 99-year lease on the [Boston and Providence Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_and_Providence_Railroad "Boston and Providence Railroad"), one of New England's earliest railroads, which had been chartered in Massachusetts in 1831 and began service between Providence and Boston in 1835. This major agreement gave the Old Colony Railroad operating rights on the busy double-tracked main line between the two capital cities, along with other branches to [Dedham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedham,_Massachusetts "Dedham, Massachusetts") and [Stoughton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stoughton,_Massachusetts "Stoughton, Massachusetts"). The deal also included use of the Boston and Providence Railroad's Park Square Station in Boston. In 1891 the OCRR signed a 99-year lease of the [Providence, Warren and Bristol Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Providence,_Warren_and_Bristol_Railroad "Providence, Warren and Bristol Railroad"). In December 1892, the OCRR signed a 99-year lease of the [Plymouth and Middleborough Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plymouth_and_Middleborough_Railroad "Plymouth and Middleborough Railroad") properties. In 1896 the OCRR acquired the [Fall River Railroad (1874)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River_Railroad_/(1874/) "Fall River Railroad (1874)"), which it had been leasing since 1882. The Old Colony Railroad was an early proponent of decorating the grounds of its train stations. By 1891, the railroad's landscaping division grew tens of thousands of plants annually at greenhouses and nurseries in [Halifax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halifax,_Massachusetts "Halifax, Massachusetts").[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Colony_Railroad#cite_note-12) ### New York, New Haven and Hartford Railroad control (1893–1969) \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Old_Colony_Railroad&action=edit§ion=6 "Edit section: New York, New Haven and Hartford Railroad control (1893–1969)")\] On March 1, 1893, the [New York, New Haven and Hartford Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York,_New_Haven_and_Hartford_Railroad "New York, New Haven and Hartford Railroad") (NYNH&H) – commonly known as the New Haven Railroad – leased the entire Old Colony system for 99 years, which by then included the leased [Boston and Providence Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_and_Providence_Railroad "Boston and Providence Railroad") and everything substantially east of it, as well as long branches northwest to Fitchburg and Lowell. Along with the lease of the [New England Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_England_Railroad "New England Railroad") in 1898, the 1893 lease arrangement gave the NYNH&H a virtual monopoly on rail transport in southern New England. On September 22, 1895, the New Haven converted all former Old Colony lines from left-hand running to right-hand running.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Colony_Railroad#cite_note-13) On April 6, 1902, a new alignment was opened from Broadway to [Crescent Avenue station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JFK/UMass_station#History "JFK/UMass station"), eliminating a grade crossing of Dorchester Avenue.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Colony_Railroad#cite_note-14) The former right-of-way was later paved as Old Colony Avenue. With the opening of Boston's [South Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Station_/(Boston/) "South Station (Boston)") in 1899, the Kneeland Street Station was taken over by the [Boston and Albany Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_and_Albany_Railroad "Boston and Albany Railroad") as a local freight office. It was demolished in 1918 after being deemed unsafe. By the 1930s, the New Haven's largest freight terminal and [only steam locomotive shop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Readville_station#Consolidation "Readville station") were both on the ex-Old Colony system; more passengers entered Boston on Old Colony lines than entered New York on the New Haven.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Colony_Railroad#cite_note-interest-15): 499  However, during its 1935–47 bankruptcy proceedings, the New Haven attempted to rid itself of unprofitable portions of the Old Colony. The New Haven's bankruptcy trustees rejected the Old Colony lease in June 1936, but were forced to continue operating it under court order. In the [88 stations case](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/88_stations_case "88 stations case"), the railroad abandoned 88 stations in Massachusetts and five in Rhode Island on a single day in 1938. The Supreme Court ruled in November 1939 (_Palmer v. Massachusetts_) that the railroad had not been given proper permission, and 32 of the stations were reopened in 1940.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Colony_Railroad#cite_note-interest-15): 500–502  After several attempts to end Old Colony passenger service - including a 1939–41 plan to outright abandon the Boston-area lines - the New Haven continued to operate the service. Whether to incorporate the Old Colony into the New Haven, and whether the Old Colony should be required to continue passenger service, continued to be argued as part of the reorganization.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Colony_Railroad#cite_note-1942report-16)[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Colony_Railroad#cite_note-1949case-17) Increased passenger and freight traffic during World War II lifted the fortunes of the New Haven.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Colony_Railroad#cite_note-150years-18): 13  The reorganization continued; the railroad was ultimately required to continue Old Colony passenger service unless losses exceeded $850,000 in a single calendar year.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Colony_Railroad#cite_note-1949case-17) The New Haven emerged from bankruptcy on September 11, 1947, and fully acquired the Old Colony a week later; the B&P was kept as a separate New Haven-owned company.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Colony_Railroad#cite_note-1949case-17)[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Colony_Railroad#cite_note-150years-18): 13  _Palmer v. Massachusetts_ had been just one of eight Supreme Court cases generated by the reorganization.[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Colony_Railroad#cite_note-19): 862  Losses on the Old Colony reached the critical value in October 1948; after threatening to discontinue all service, the New Haven cut back to a 26-train peak-only schedule on the Boston Group in March 1949.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Colony_Railroad#cite_note-1949case-17)[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Colony_Railroad#cite_note-150years-18): 13, 96 Under the 1951–1954 presidency of [Frederic C. Dumaine Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederic_C._Dumaine_Jr. "Frederic C. Dumaine Jr."), the New Haven increased passenger service, using new [Budd Rail Diesel Cars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Budd_Rail_Diesel_Car "Budd Rail Diesel Car") to reduce costs.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Colony_Railroad#cite_note-150years-18): 13  Boston service reached 86 trains in April 1954.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Colony_Railroad#cite_note-150years-18): 96  As losses mounted, Boston-area railroads made major cuts in the late 1950s. All service to Taunton, Fall River, and New Bedford (which used the B&P rather than the Old Colony mainline) ended in 1958.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Colony_Railroad#cite_note-150years-18): 36  All remaining year-round Old Colony Division service ended on June 30, 1959, after the completion of the [Southeast Expressway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeast_Expressway_/(Boston/) "Southeast Expressway (Boston)"), though limited seasonal service continued for several more years.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Colony_Railroad#cite_note-150years-18): 96 [\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Colony_Railroad#cite_note-netransit-20) The NYNH&H merged into [Penn Central](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penn_Central "Penn Central") in 1969, which in turn merged into [Conrail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conrail "Conrail") in 1976.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Colony_Railroad#cite_note-netransit-20) Since the early 1970s, [Amtrak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amtrak "Amtrak") has provided passenger service from South Station in Boston over the former [Boston and Providence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_and_Providence_Railroad "Boston and Providence Railroad") lines of the Old Colony Railroad. Since December 2000, Amtrak has also used this line for the [Acela Express](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acela_Express "Acela Express") passenger rail service to Washington, D.C. Between 1986 and 1996 Amtrak also operated regular passenger service between New York City and Hyannis on Cape Cod during the summer months.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Colony_Railroad#cite_note-21) With the establishment of Conrail, freight service continued over various portions of the former Old Colony network after 1976. Beginning in 1982, the [Bay Colony Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bay_Colony_Railroad "Bay Colony Railroad") provided freight service on various lines which the Commonwealth of Massachusetts had purchased from Conrail, including lines on Cape Cod and in [Middlesex County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middlesex_County,_Massachusetts "Middlesex County, Massachusetts"). Since 1999, [CSX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CSX "CSX") has provided freight service over several portions of the former Old Colony Railroad network, including lines in [Taunton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taunton,_Massachusetts "Taunton, Massachusetts"), Fall River, New Bedford and [Leominster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leominster,_Massachusetts "Leominster, Massachusetts"). Since 2008, the [Massachusetts Coastal Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Coastal_Railroad "Massachusetts Coastal Railroad") has taken over operation of the state-owned freight lines on Cape Cod from the Bay Colony Railroad. The [Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Bay_Transportation_Authority "Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority") (MBTA) was formed in 1964 to subsidize remaining commuter rail operations. Service was continued on the ex-B&P lines – now the [Providence/Stoughton Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Providence/Stoughton_Line "Providence/Stoughton Line") and portions of the [Needham Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Needham_Line "Needham Line"). The [MBTA Commuter Rail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_Commuter_Rail "MBTA Commuter Rail") system has been expanded since the 1980s. Service was restored on the [Plymouth/Kingston Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plymouth/Kingston_Line "Plymouth/Kingston Line") (now the [Kingston Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_Line "Kingston Line")) and [Middleborough/Lakeville Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middleborough/Lakeville_Line "Middleborough/Lakeville Line") (now the [Fall River/New Bedford Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line "Fall River/New Bedford Line")) – collectively known as the **Old Colony Lines** – in 1997, and on the [Greenbush Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenbush_Line "Greenbush Line") in 2007. Seasonal [CapeFlyer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CapeFlyer "CapeFlyer") excursion service between Boston and Hyannis, operated by the MBTA, began in 2013. The [Fall River/New Bedford Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line "Fall River/New Bedford Line") opened as an extension of the Middleborough/Lakeville Line in 2025.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Colony_Railroad#cite_note-netransit-20) Two portions of the former Old Colony network are used for [tourist trains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourist_train "Tourist train"): the [Cape Cod Central Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Cod_Central_Railroad "Cape Cod Central Railroad") on Cape Cod, and the [Newport and Narragansett Bay Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newport_and_Narragansett_Bay_Railroad "Newport and Narragansett Bay Railroad") on Aquidneck Island. Between 1986 and 2016, the [Old Colony & Fall River Railroad Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Colony_%26_Fall_River_Railroad_Museum "Old Colony & Fall River Railroad Museum") operated in Fall River.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Colony_Railroad#cite_note-Holtzman-22) The museum had four train cars and exhibits.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Colony_Railroad#cite_note-Holtzman-22) Presidents of the Old Colony Railroad ------------------------------------- \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Old_Colony_Railroad&action=edit§ion=8 "Edit section: Presidents of the Old Colony Railroad")\] * John Sever (June 1844 to December 1845)[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Colony_Railroad#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFisher1919152-23) * [Nathan Carruth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nathan_Carruth "Nathan Carruth") (December 1845 to January 1848)[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Colony_Railroad#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFisher1919152-23) * Elias Hasket Derby (January 1848 to April 1850)[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Colony_Railroad#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFisher1919152-23) * Francis B. Passenger Rail Service Returns To Massachusetts South Coast
===========================================================

March 25, 2025

### Share this:

*   [Tweet](https://twitter.com/share)
*   [![Image 5](https://assets.pinterest.com/images/pidgets/pinit_fg_en_rect_gray_20.png)](https://www.pinterest.com/pin/create/button/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.capecod.com%2Fnewscenter%2Fsouth-coast-rail-stations-have-opened%2F&media=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.capecod.com%2Fwp-content%2Fuploads%2FNWS_MBTA_BCM121118.jpg&description=Passenger%20Rail%20Service%20Returns%20To%20Massachusetts%20South%20Coast)
    
*   [Click to email a link to a friend (Opens in new window) Email](https://www.capecod.com/cdn-cgi/l/email-protection#)

![Image 6](https://www.capecod.com/wp-content/uploads/NWS_MBTA_BCM121118-300x275.jpg)

NEW BEDFORD – Massachusetts officials celebrated the start of the MBTA’s South Coast Rail on Monday.

To entice passengers, the service is being offered for free through the end of this month, and parking is temporarily no-cost, also.

The commuter rail line formerly known as Middleborough/Lakeville has been renamed the Fall River/New Bedford Line to reflect the new stops.

Additionally, the T says commuter rail trains will no-longer stop at Lakeville Station, and that it will only service the seasonal CapeFLYER. A new station is planned to open in Middleborough.

“Our administration isn’t kicking the can down the road when it comes to delivering the transportation system that our residents deserve. That’s exactly how we approached the South Coast Rail project. After years of delays, we took this challenge head on and delivered for the people of the South Coast and our entire state will benefit,” said Governor Maura Healey.

“The start of rail service will give people more options for how to get around, where to live and where to work. It means less traffic congestion and shorter commutes, giving people more time back with their loved ones. And it will bring more customers to local businesses and cultural attractions in Southeastern Mass,” Healey added.

Southeast Massachusetts is also currently serviced by the Kingston commuter rail line, formerly known as the Plymouth/Kingston Line. The T station in Plymouth closed in 2021.

Southeast Mass and the Cape have a history of passenger rail service that dates back to the mid-19th century.

_**By Jim McCabe, CapeCod.com NewsCenter**_

ARRA Fact Sheet: MBTA Wind Energy Generation Turbines
=====================================================

**Project:** MBTA Wind Energy Generation Turbines

**City**: Kingston and Bridgewater

**State**: Massachusetts

**ARRA Award Amount**: $2.5 Million

**Program**: TIGGER (Wind Energy)

**Description**:

FTA has approved $2.5 million in competitively selected TIGGER funds to the Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority (MBTA) for installation of two renewable wind energy generation turbines to be located at the Kingston Layover Facility at the terminus of the Kingston/Plymouth Commuter Rail branch and the Bridgewater Station on the Middleborough/Lakeville Commuter Rail branch. The proposed wind energy equipment includes a 100 kW turbine located at the Kingston Layover and a 600 kW turbine located at the Bridgewater Station.

The MBTA is the largest single electricity consumer in Massachusetts, consuming nine percent of all electricity consumed in the state. With the installation of renewable wind energy turbines such as the ones proposed in Kingston and Bridgewater in southeastern Massachusetts, the MBTA will be able to generate power to operate its own facilities or return power back to the regional grid, thereby providing clean energy to the region. Both facilities currently consume energy to support the plugging-in of trains for storage, maintenance and passenger waiting facilities. The annual electricity use at both facilities is 2,815,738 kWh. Not only will this investment allow the MBTA to save 75 percent of energy consumption at these locations, but also, in virtue of the high visibility placement of the wind turbines at major transportation nodes, serve as a model for use of green technologies region wide.

# Executive Summary 

In September 1997 the Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority (MBTA) reinstituted passenger service on two routes of the former Old Colony Railroad system. Previous passenger service on these lines had ended in 1959. This report presents the final results of a study conducted for the MBTA by the Central Transportation Planning Staff (CTPS) of the impacts that restoration of Old Colony passenger service has had on other transportation facilities. The results of a survey of Old Colony riders conducted by CTPS in September 1998 are presented in a separate report. DESCRIPTION OF OLD COLONY LINES The present Old Colony lines consist of two branches: the Middleborough/Lakeville Line and the Plymouth/Kingston Line. These lines share track between South Station in Boston and Braintree station, and connect with Red Line rapid transit service at those two points and at Quincy Center. Otherwise, they are separate. The Plymouth/ Kingston Line divides further at the outer end, with branches to terminals in Kingston and in Plymouth. All three outer terminals on the Old Colony Lines are about 35 miles from downtown Boston. The Middleborough/Lakeville Line has six stations south of Braintree and the Plymouth/Kingston Line has seven. Since November 1997 the weekday schedule on the Middleborough/Lakeville Line has provided 12 round trips, including four inbound in the A.M. peak and four outbound in the P.M. peak. (A fifth inbound trip arrives in Boston just before the start of the A.M. peak.) The weekday schedule on the Plymouth/Kingston Line has provided 15 round trips, including five inbound in the

> IMPACTS ON OTHER TRANSPORTATION FACILITIES

The 1998 survey found that 81 % of Old Colony riders were using the service for trips that they had previously made by some other means. (Some of the other 19% had coincidental changes in travel requirements after 1997 and would have begun traveling by other means if Old Colony service had not been provided.) Of the riders who had switched from other travel methods, the largest group (40%) consisted of former rapid transit riders. Diversions from driving alone for the entire distance were second (28%), followed by diversions from private carrier express bus routes (20%). Most of the rest came from older commuter rail lines and carpools, with under 2%  coming  from commuter boats. With no other changes, the older transportation services and facilities would have been expected to show ridership losses equal to the number of Old Colony passengers diverted from each. Such was not the case, however. The Old Colony lines, like all lines in the MBTA commuter rail system, are used predominantly for work travel to and from Boston and Cambridge. The Old Colony lines opened during a time of continued growth in such travel. Therefore, on many of the older alternatives, diversions to Old Colony service have been largely or entirely offset by new users. Impacts on prior modes are summarized below, in order of their importance as sources of Old Colony riders. 

Rapid Transit

MBTA Bus Service 

The MBTA has never operated bus service through to downtown Boston from the present Old Colony service area. Any Old Colony riders who formerly rode MBTA busses would have used them in combination with rapid transit service, and would be included in the rapid transit diversion totals. The locations of Old Colony stations relative to MBTA feeder bus routes are such that the majority of people who rode busses to the Red Line before 1997 would still find doing so more convenient than switching to Old Colony trains. The ridership losses on most MBTA bus routes in the area were therefore insignificant. The largest ridership loss apparently attributable to Old Colony diversions from any one route was a drop of about 70 riders each way on the segment of Route 240 south of Crawford Square, Randolph. A secondary effect was loss of about 80 interline riders each way between Routes 238 and 240 as a result of reconfiguring these routes to serve the Holbrook/Randolph Station. The new route segment serves about 60 new riders each way, but most of them are not using the commuter rail line. 

CONCLUSION 

Because the Old Colony lines began operating during a time of rising demand for transportation to Boston from the area they now serve, most of the riders who switched to Old Colony trains from older transportation facilities have been replaced by new users of those facilities. Therefore, it can be concluded that Old Colony trains have helped to reduce the amount of congestion that would otherwise have occurred on the other alternatives. The most notable exception to the general trends has been on private carrier bus routes to Boston from the Old Colony service area. As a group, these bus lines lost nearly 40% of their riders in the first year of Old Colony operations. With a few exceptions, they have continued losing riders since then, and have reduced capacity accordingly. Among former bus users, as among Old Colony riders in general, nearly 70% cited convenience as a reason for using Old Colony service. Thus, although many Old Colony riders are not new transit users, they are being provided with a more convenient travel alternative than was formerly available to them.

The findings in this report should prove useful not only in documenting the Old Colony impacts but also in predicting impacts of future rail extensions in greater Boston and elsewhere.

Results of Before and After Passenger Counts 

Because the cities and towns now served by the Old Colony Lines formerly accounted for a small part of Wollaston ridership, it is difficult to distinguish impacts of the Old Colony service from normal day-to-day ridership variation. Riders shifting from Wollaston would, however, have had to pay higher inbound fares (full fare of $1.70 vs. $0.85) at Quincy Center, Quincy Adams, or Braintree and would also have to pay exit fares at the latter two. The outer three stations also had higher parking fees than Wollaston ($2.50 vs. $2.00). The extra cost would be a disincentive to station-shifting for passengers already accustomed to going to Wollaston. Outbound Wollaston alightings showed an overall gain of 16%, with over two-thirds of the absolute gain occurring in the P.M. peak. In the 1997 counts, all-day inbound ons at Wollaston exceeded outbound offs by 580 (18%). This explanation is supported by the results at Quincy Center, where outbound offs in the 1997 counts exceeded inbound ons by 880. In the 1998 counts, inbound ons at Wollaston exceeded outbound offs by 213, but outbound offs at Quincy Center exceeded inbound ons by 635. This indicates that there was an increase in the proportion of Wollaston boarding passengers also alighting at Wollaston. Although such a change is not clearly related to Old Colony service, it does suggest that there was a significant difference between travel habits of W ollaston riders in 1997 and 1998. Such a large change is more likely to have resulted from a turnover in the riders using the station than in the habits of the same riders, so Old Colony service may indeed have been a contributing factor.
